meta.title: NUR 868 board-style bank: temperature, vigilance and alarms, breathing circuits, respiratory monitoring, ventilators
meta.answer_format: a = zero-based indexes into c; select = number of correct choices

questions.q: Per the lecture, hypothermia is defined as a core temperature below what value?
questions.exp: Wolpaw's quiz answer is a core temp below 35°C. Note the lecture ties 35–36°C to harm already.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 4

questions.q: A core temperature of 35.5°C during surgery is associated with which change in morbid cardiac outcomes?
questions.exp: the lecture: core temps of 35–36°C triple morbid cardiac outcomes and SSI and raise blood loss, so harm starts above the formal 35°C cutoff.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 2

questions.q: Cold sensation travels mainly on which fibers?
questions.exp: Cold travels on A-delta fibers; warmth on unmyelinated C fibers, with some overlap.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 4

questions.q: Warmth sensation travels mainly on which fibers?
questions.exp: Heat and warmth receptors signal through unmyelinated C fibers; cold uses A-delta.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 4

questions.q: Thermal afferents ascend to the hypothalamus through which pathway?
c: Corticospinal tracts in the lateral cord
Dorsal columns in the posterior cord
Spinocerebellar tracts in the lateral cord
Spinothalamic tracts in the anterior cord
questions.exp: Thermal input rises in the anterior spinothalamic tracts; some processing also occurs in the cord itself.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 4

questions.q: Which specific region is the primary thermoregulatory control center?
c: Preoptic area of the anterior hypothalamus
Supraoptic nucleus of the posterior hypothalamus
questions.exp: Wolpaw: the preoptic area in the anterior hypothalamus integrates peripheral and central thermal input.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 27

questions.q: Which receptor proteins are the most important thermal sensors?
c: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on skin nerve endings
questions.exp: the lecture: TRP proteins are the most important heat and cold receptors.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 4

questions.q: On this thermoregulatory response curve, which numbered point marks the threshold?
questions.exp: The threshold is the core temperature where the response begins (3). The slope (2) is the gain, and the plateau (1) is maximum intensity.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slides 3, 4

questions.q: On this curve, the steepness of segment 2 represents what?
questions.exp: Gain is response intensity per °C change, the slope. Threshold is where the response starts.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slides 3, 4

questions.q: A drug shifts point 3 on this curve to a lower core temperature without changing segment 2. What has the drug done?
c: Lowered the threshold; the response starts at a colder temperature
Raised the threshold; the response starts sooner
Raised the gain; the response grows stronger with each °C
Lowered the maximum intensity of the response
questions.exp: Moving the start point left means a colder temperature is needed to trigger the response: a lower threshold, gain unchanged. This is what volatiles and propofol do to vasoconstriction and shivering.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slides 3, 4

questions.q: Which three components make up temperature regulation?
c: Afferent input, central control, efferent response
questions.exp: Afferent input, central (hypothalamic) control, and efferent response. Threshold and gain describe each response.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 3

questions.q: Sweating is mediated by which nerves?
questions.exp: Sweat glands get sympathetic innervation that releases acetylcholine (postganglionic cholinergic).
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 5

questions.q: In a room hotter than core temperature, which is the only mechanism that can still remove heat?
questions.exp: When ambient exceeds core, radiation and convection add heat. Evaporation of sweat is the only route left.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 5

questions.q: Which mediator is NOT listed among those involved in active cutaneous vasodilation?
questions.exp: The lecture lists NO, VIP, substance P, histamine, and prostaglandins. Norepinephrine drives vasoconstriction.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 5

questions.q: Which thermoregulatory responses are the most effective quantitatively?
questions.exp: Behavioral responses (clothing, moving, changing the room) are strongest, and general anesthesia removes them.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 5

questions.q: Arteriovenous shunt vasoconstriction in response to cold is mediated by which receptors?
questions.exp: Cold-induced cutaneous AV shunt vasoconstriction is α1/α2 mediated. β3 drives brown fat.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 6

questions.q: Shivering increases metabolic heat production by about how much?
questions.exp: Shivering raises heat production 50–100%. The 135–468% figure is the rise in O2 demand.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 6

questions.q: Postanesthetic shivering can increase oxygen demand by how much?
questions.exp: the lecture (highlighted): shivering can raise O2 demand by 135% to 468%.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 11

questions.q: Shivering occurs over which core temperature range?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: shivering occurs at 32–35°C and stops below about 32°C.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 25

questions.q: A trauma patient's core temp is 30.5°C and there is no shivering. What best explains this?
c: The patient has reached thermal neutrality
Shivering never occurs in adults under GA
Shivering is blocked by the trauma itself
questions.exp: Below about 32°C shivering fails, so absence of shivering here signals deeper hypothermia, not recovery.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 25

questions.q: Which is NOT a listed downside of shivering?
questions.exp: Wolpaw lists increased metabolic demand, O2 consumption, and ICP. Shivering raises ICP, not lowers it.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 25

questions.q: Newborns produce heat mainly through which mechanism?
c: Increased voluntary muscle tone and movement
Active cutaneous vasodilation of the trunk
Shivering of large skeletal muscle groups
questions.exp: Shivering is absent in newborns, so they rely on nonshivering thermogenesis, which doubles heat production.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 6

questions.q: Nonshivering thermogenesis is mediated by which receptor?
questions.exp: β3 receptors activate brown fat, where thermogenin uncouples metabolism to produce heat.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 6

questions.q: What does thermogenin do in brown fat?
c: Constricts skin vessels to hold heat
Increases ATP production for muscle contraction
Uncouples oxidation so substrate becomes heat directly
questions.exp: Thermogenin is an uncoupling protein; energy that would make ATP is released as heat.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 6

questions.q: Nonshivering thermogenesis changes infant heat production by about how much?
questions.exp: the lecture: nonshivering thermogenesis doubles heat production in infants.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 6

questions.q: What is the purpose of piloerection?
c: Trapping a warm layer of air next to the skin
Increasing radiant heat loss from the skin
Increasing sweat evaporation from the skin
Stimulating brown fat beneath the skin
questions.exp: Goosebumps trap air close to the skin to create an insulating warm layer.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 26

questions.q: On this core temperature curve after induction of GA, which numbered phase is caused by redistribution?
questions.exp: Phase 1 is the rapid drop from core-to-periphery redistribution. Phase 2 is the slow linear loss; phase 3 is the plateau.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 7

questions.q: What drives the slope of numbered phase 2 on this curve?
c: Heat loss exceeding metabolic heat production
Redistribution of heat from core to periphery
Shivering at the start of surgery
questions.exp: GA cuts metabolic rate 20–30%, so ongoing losses exceed production and temperature falls slowly and linearly.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 7

questions.q: Under GA, what most likely produces numbered phase 3 on this curve?
c: Return of behavioral responses as anesthesia lightens
Increased metabolic rate from the volatile anesthetic
Sweating stopping once core temp falls below 36°C
Vasoconstriction once the lowered threshold is reached
questions.exp: The plateau appears when core temp falls to the anesthetic-lowered vasoconstriction threshold and vasoconstriction limits further loss. Neuraxial blocks this, so the curve may not plateau.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 7

questions.q: In the first phase after induction, core temperature typically falls by about how much?
questions.exp: the lecture: an initial rapid drop of about 0.5–1.5°C over roughly 30 minutes.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 7

questions.q: During the linear phase of GA hypothermia, core temp falls at about what rate?
questions.exp: Phase 2 is a slow linear reduction of about 0.3°C/hr.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 7

questions.q: General anesthesia decreases metabolic rate by about how much?
questions.exp: GA lowers metabolic rate 20–30%, which is why heat loss outpaces production.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 7

questions.q: During the first hour after induction, core temp drops about 1.5°C mainly because of what?
c: Conduction to the cold OR table surface
Radiant heat loss to the cold OR walls
Redistribution of heat from core to periphery
Evaporation from the airway and skin prep
questions.exp: Wolpaw's quiz answer: redistribution after anesthetic vasodilation, not environmental loss.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 15

questions.q: If the OR were kept at 37°C, about what would the patient's core temp be after one hour of GA?
c: 37°C, since there is no gradient to the room
questions.exp: Redistribution still moves heat from core to periphery, so core falls toward mean body temp (about 35.5°C) even with no environmental loss.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 17

questions.q: Volatile anesthetics have which effect on thermoregulatory thresholds?
c: Lower the sweating threshold markedly, with no effect on cold responses
Little effect on sweating, but lower vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds
Raise the vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds
questions.exp: Volatiles, N2O, propofol, and opioids barely change sweating but significantly lower the cold-response thresholds.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 7

questions.q: How do volatile agents, propofol, and opioids affect cold-response thresholds? Select 2.
questions.exp: They significantly lower vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds with minimal effect on sweating.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 7

questions.q: How does neuraxial anesthesia compare with GA in its effect on thermoregulation?
c: It has minimal effect because the brain is unaffected
It improves cold responses below the block
It impairs thermoregulation to about the same extent
questions.exp: the lecture: neuraxial affects thermoregulation to the same extent as GA.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 8

questions.q: The reduction in vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds with neuraxial anesthesia is proportional to what?
questions.exp: The impairment is a linear function of block height, likely from blocked tonic cold signals from the lower body.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 8

questions.q: Why may core temperature fail to plateau during neuraxial anesthesia?
c: Redistribution is absent because the block causes no vasodilation
Peripheral vasoconstriction below the block is inhibited
questions.exp: The GA plateau depends on vasoconstriction. Neuraxial blocks it in the lower body, so temperature can keep falling.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 8

questions.q: A patient under spinal anesthesia is 35°C but says she feels warm. What best explains this?
c: Absent tonic cold signals from the blocked area are read as warmth
Her core temperature reading is falsely low
The spinal raised her vasoconstriction threshold above normal
questions.exp: Neuraxial patients often don't feel cold even when hypothermic; the central controller may misread missing cold input as warmth.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 8

questions.q: Which are mechanisms by which neuraxial anesthesia impairs thermoregulation? Select 3.
c: Raised vasoconstriction threshold proportional to block height
Impaired autonomic defenses below the block
questions.exp: the lecture lists three: reduced discomfort, central threshold reduction (linear with block height), and blocked autonomic defenses.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 8

questions.q: Which mechanism accounts for most intraoperative heat loss?
questions.exp: Radiation accounts for about 40%; convection about 30% is second.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slides 9, 10

questions.q: Which mechanism is the second largest source of intraoperative heat loss?
questions.exp: Convection (about 30%) is second after radiation (about 40%).
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 10

questions.q: Evaporation accounts for about what share of intraoperative heat loss?
questions.exp: Evaporation from open cavities and the respiratory tract is about 8–10%.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 10

questions.q: Radiant heat loss is proportional to the temperature difference raised to what power?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: radiant loss scales with the temperature difference to the 4th power, which is why radiation dominates.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 18

questions.q: Infusing a liter of cold IV fluid causes heat loss mainly by which mechanism?
questions.exp: Direct contact between the intravascular compartment and colder fluid is conduction.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 10

questions.q: Covering the patient with drapes most effectively reduces which mechanism?
questions.exp: The lecture says clothing and drapes are effective at decreasing convective loss (the note adds radiation).
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 10

questions.q: On this figure, which numbered arrow represents conduction?
questions.exp: Arrow 4 shows heat moving into the table by direct contact. 1 is evaporation, 2 convection, 3 radiation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 9

questions.q: Which numbered mechanism on this figure causes the most intraoperative heat loss?
questions.exp: Mechanism 3 is radiation, about 40% of losses.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slides 9, 10

questions.q: A long open laparotomy most increases heat loss through which numbered mechanism?
questions.exp: Mechanism 1 is evaporation, which rises with open body cavities (the note: "think total full open belly").
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slides 9, 10

questions.q: Air currents around the patient cause loss through which numbered mechanism?
questions.exp: Mechanism 2 is convection: heat lost to the air immediately surrounding the body.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 10

questions.q: Hypothermia impairs platelet aggregation by reducing release of which mediator?
questions.exp: Hypothermia reduces thromboxane release (the slide's "A3" is a typo for A2), reversibly impairing aggregation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 11

questions.q: A temperature drop from 37 to 35.5°C increases average blood loss by about how much?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: about 500 mL more, from slower clotting enzymes and platelet dysfunction.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 9

questions.q: A hypothermic patient is oozing diffusely, but PT/PTT are normal. Why?
c: PT/PTT are falsely prolonged at low temperatures
Hypothermia only affects platelets, not clotting factors
Hypothermia causes no coagulopathy when the core is above 34°C
Labs warm the sample to 37°C, hiding the hypothermic coagulopathy
questions.exp: Coag tests run at 37°C, so the effect of cold on enzyme activity disappears in the lab. Warm the patient.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 9

questions.q: A drop from 37 to 35°C raises surgical site infection risk by about how much?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: SSI risk increases 2–3 fold.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 8

questions.q: Which mechanisms explain higher SSI risk with hypothermia? Select 3.
c: Decreased O2 delivery to the wound
Increased O2 delivery to the wound
Vasodilation flooding the wound with neutrophils
questions.exp: Vasoconstriction lowers blood, O2, and PMN delivery and reduces oxidative killing (superoxide).
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 8

questions.q: Intraoperative temperature falling to 35°C increases hospital stay by about how long?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: about 2.5 days longer.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 10

questions.q: Normothermia compared with 35°C reduces cardiac morbidity by about how much?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: about a 55% reduction.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 11

questions.q: Per Wolpaw, hypothermia harms the heart mainly through which mechanism?
c: Arrhythmias and hypertension from catecholamine release
Direct myocardial cooling that causes infarction and asystole
questions.exp: Wolpaw specifically states "NOT shivering"; morbidity is from arrhythmias and hypertension.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 11

questions.q: Which is NOT an adverse effect of intraoperative hypothermia?
questions.exp: Wolpaw's quiz answer: DVT/PE risk is not increased.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 7

questions.q: How does hypothermia affect MAC?
c: It has no effect on MAC
questions.exp: Anesthetic requirement falls as temperature falls (lecture figure 15% per °C; most references about 5%).
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 12

questions.q: At 35°C, the duration of vecuronium and rocuronium is prolonged by up to about how much?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: up to 60% longer. Slowed metabolism and clearance extend NMB duration.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 12

questions.q: Per the Wolpaw lecture, MAC decreases by about how much per 1°C drop?
questions.exp: The lecture answer is 15%. Many references cite about 5%, so watch which number your exam uses.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 12

questions.q: Which are listed adverse effects of hypothermia? Select 3.
c: Decreased urine output from vasopressin release
questions.exp: Wolpaw's list includes renal injury, electrolyte disturbances, hypoglycemia, cold diuresis, and rhabdo. the lecture adds slowed drug metabolism.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 13

questions.q: How does hypothermia affect hepatic drug metabolism?
c: It has no effect on hepatic enzymes
It slows metabolism, prolonging drug effects
It speeds metabolism, shortening drug effects
It speeds only phase II reactions
questions.exp: Enzyme activity drops with temperature, so drugs last longer.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 11

questions.q: Postanesthetic shivering occurs in up to what share of patients?
questions.exp: the lecture: up to 40%.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 11

questions.q: Which patients have a higher risk of unintended perioperative hypothermia? Select 2.
c: Middle-aged adults with normal fluid shifts
questions.exp: Prolonged surgery, extremes of age, big fluid shifts, severe trauma, and extensive burns raise risk.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 11

questions.q: On this ECG, which numbered deflection is characteristic of hypothermia?
questions.exp: Deflection 3 is the J (Osborn) wave, an extra hump right after the QRS.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 14

questions.q: The Osborn wave is usually not seen until core temperature falls to about what?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: usually not until around 32°C.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 14

questions.q: What is another name for the J wave seen in hypothermia?
questions.exp: J wave and Osborn wave are the same finding.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 14

questions.q: Compared with an equal degree of hypothermia, hyperthermia is:
questions.exp: the lecture: hyperthermia is more dangerous than similar degrees of hypothermia.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 12

questions.q: What is the most common cause of intraoperative hyperthermia?
questions.exp: Overwarming, especially in long cases, is most common.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 12

questions.q: Four hours into a case under a full-body forced-air warmer, temp has slowly risen to 38.1°C. EtCO2 and HR are stable. FIRST action?
c: Turn down or remove the forced-air warmer and recheck
Switch to TIVA, give dantrolene, and call for the MH cart
questions.exp: A slow late rise with stable EtCO2 and HR fits overwarming, not MH (instructor note).
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 12

questions.q: Which finding best distinguishes early MH from iatrogenic overwarming?
c: A forced-air warmer set to high
Flushed, warm skin over the trunk
Core temperature that reaches 38°C late in the case
questions.exp: MH is hypermetabolic: CO2 production climbs early. Overwarming raises temp without a CO2 surge.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 12

questions.q: Which are listed consequences of hyperthermia? Select 3.
questions.exp: Hyperthermia raises metabolic demand and CV stress and risks coagulopathy, organ dysfunction, neuropathy, and seizures.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 12

questions.q: Which drug class carries up to a 2% risk of neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: antipsychotics carry up to 2% risk.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 33

questions.q: Stopping which drug can trigger NMS?
questions.exp: Abrupt cessation of dopamine agonists (amantadine, bromocriptine, levodopa) can cause NMS.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 33

questions.q: An antiemetic linked to NMS in the lecture is:
questions.exp: Reglan (metoclopramide) is a dopamine antagonist listed as an NMS cause.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 33

questions.q: Typical onset of NMS is:
questions.exp: NMS is late in onset, unlike serotonin syndrome (within 6 hours).
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 33

questions.q: What is the dantrolene dosing range listed for NMS?
c: 2.5 mg/kg IV push repeated to 10 mg/kg
questions.exp: Wolpaw lists 2–3 mg/kg/day up to 10 mg/kg/day for NMS.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 33

questions.q: Serotonin syndrome typically begins within how long?
questions.exp: Serotonin syndrome is abrupt, within about 6 hours.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 34

questions.q: A patient on an MAOI gets meperidine in PACU and develops fever, clonus, and hyperreflexia within 2 hours. Which treatment is least likely to help?
questions.exp: This is serotonin syndrome. Dantrolene doesn't help; treat with drug removal, supportive care, benzos, and paralysis if severe.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 34

questions.q: Which drugs can cause serotonin syndrome? Select 3.
questions.exp: The list includes SSRIs, MAOIs, TCAs, tryptophan, ritonavir, lithium, triptans, meperidine, fentanyl, and methylene blue.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 34

questions.q: Which feature best distinguishes serotonin syndrome from NMS?
c: Hyperreflexia and clonus with abrupt onset
Recent exposure to a psychiatric medication
questions.exp: Both cause fever, AMS, and autonomic instability. Serotonin syndrome brings clonus and hyperreflexia, fast onset, and less rigidity.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slides 33, 34

questions.q: In severe serotonin syndrome not controlled by benzodiazepines, the lecture suggests considering what?
questions.exp: Severe cases may need paralysis (with intubation) to stop muscle hyperactivity and heat.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 34

questions.q: Prewarming before induction reduces redistribution hypothermia by doing what?
c: Raising the vasoconstriction threshold before induction
questions.exp: Warmer peripheries mean less heat flows out of the core when vasodilation occurs.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 13

questions.q: Per Course materials, how long should skin be warmed before induction to prevent redistribution hypothermia?
questions.exp: the lecture: 30 minutes of skin surface warming. Wolpaw says 2 hours for full effect.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 13

questions.q: Per Wolpaw, how long does prewarming need to be fully effective?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: prewarming raises mean body temp but needs about 2 hours.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 21

questions.q: What ambient temperature is recommended for prewarming children in the induction room and OR?
questions.exp: the lecture: 26°C for 30–40 minutes is safe and effective.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 13

questions.q: One liter of room-temperature crystalloid lowers mean body temperature by about how much?
questions.exp: the lecture: about 0.25°C per liter (or unit of refrigerated PRBCs), up to 1°C.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 14

questions.q: IV fluids should be warmed to what range?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: 38–42°C.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 23

questions.q: Per the lecture, what is the most basic method for maintaining normothermia in the OR?
c: Forced-air warming over the upper body
questions.exp: Raising room temperature is the most basic (highlighted), used in liver transplant and major trauma.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 15

questions.q: What is the easiest method to decrease cutaneous heat loss?
c: Passive insulation of the skin surface
questions.exp: Highlighted: passive insulation (blankets, drapes) is easiest.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 15

questions.q: Warm cotton blankets reduce radiant heat loss by up to about how much?
questions.exp: the lecture and the instructor note: about 30%.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 15

questions.q: What is the most effective NONINVASIVE method of warming a patient?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: forced-air warming (Bair Hugger).
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 22

questions.q: What is the most effective overall method of warming a patient?
questions.exp: CPB rewarms about 9°C/hr, the fastest listed.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 23

questions.q: Why should a warming device go on top of the patient rather than underneath?
c: Top warmers block conduction to the table
Heat rises, so an underbody warmer mostly warms the table
Body weight compresses the tissue, so less blood flows there
questions.exp: Compressed dependent tissue has little blood flow to carry the heat in, and it's more prone to burns.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 22

questions.q: Forced-air warmers work by doing what?
c: Transferring heat by conduction from heated coils in the blanket
Reducing evaporation by humidifying the skin
Raising core temperature by warming inspired gas
Preventing radiant loss while transferring heat by convection
questions.exp: They block radiation and actively add heat by convection.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 16

questions.q: About how fast can forced-air warming raise temperature, versus CPB?
questions.exp: Instructor notes: forced air about 2–3°C/hr; CPB about 9°C/hr.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 23

questions.q: For severe hypothermia with cardiac instability when ECMO is unavailable, the rewarming table lists which technique (about 9°C/hr)?
questions.exp: CPB is listed for HT III with instability or HT IV when ECMO isn't available.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 24

questions.q: Which rewarming technique in the table provides cardiac support at about 6°C/hr?
questions.exp: VA ECMO gives cardiac support at about 6°C/hr; VV ECMO (4°C/hr) does not support the heart.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 24

questions.q: An esophageal stethoscope with a temperature probe is an example of what?
questions.exp: the lecture: esophageal stethoscope/temperature probes are thermistors.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 18

questions.q: Thermocouples and thermistors are accurate to about what range?
questions.exp: They're cheap, stable, and reproducible to 0.1–0.2°C.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 18

questions.q: Why are liquid crystal skin thermometers poor choices intraoperatively?
c: They are too expensive for routine OR use
Skin and core temps diverge during rapid changes
questions.exp: Skin temperature poorly tracks core, particularly under changing physiology.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 19

questions.q: Which site is closest to what the hypothalamus sees, outside of blood?
questions.exp: Wolpaw's quiz answer (highlighted): distal esophageal.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slides 29, 30

questions.q: What is the most accurate overall site for core temperature?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: PA catheter or high IJ is most accurate overall; distal esophagus is best outside blood.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 31

questions.q: Which are core temperature sites? Select 3.
questions.exp: Core: PA, distal esophagus, tympanic membrane, nasopharynx. Oral, rectal, and bladder are intermediate.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 20

questions.q: During rapid rewarming on bypass, which site is least reliable for core temperature?
questions.exp: Intermediate sites (oral, rectal, bladder) lag during rapid thermal changes; core sites stay reliable.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 20

questions.q: Which site is decent for core temp but carries a bleeding risk?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: nasopharyngeal is decent but can cause bleeding.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 31

questions.q: When is human body temperature normally lowest?
questions.exp: Minimum 4–8 am; maximum 4–6 pm.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 35

questions.q: About what share of postoperative fevers are NOT caused by infection?
questions.exp: Wolpaw: 67% of postop fevers and 50% of ICU fevers are not infectious.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 35

questions.q: Which statement about fever in hospitalized patients is true per the lecture?
c: All fevers above 38.5°C should be treated
Higher fevers reliably point to a bacterial infection source
Fever severity does not correlate with likelihood of infection
Treating fever below 40°C is always beneficial
questions.exp: Severity doesn't predict infection, and treating fever below 40°C may cause harm.
questions.ref: Course materials: Wolpaw, Temperature Regulation: slide 35

questions.q: Compared with GA alone, what does neuraxial anesthesia change about the temperature curve?
c: There is no initial drop, only a linear decline
The initial drop is larger, then temperature rises
Temperature rises after the drop because vasodilation is blocked
The initial drop is similar, but the plateau may not develop
questions.exp: Both start with redistribution and a linear decline; neuraxial blocks vasoconstriction, so no plateau.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slides 7, 8

questions.q: Before a long case, prewarming for 30 minutes is planned. Which effect is expected?
c: Prevention of the linear phase entirely
A rise in core temperature that offsets the linear phase
No change in the initial drop, but a faster plateau
A smaller initial drop in core temperature after induction
questions.exp: Prewarming targets redistribution (phase 1). Losses still exceed production afterward, so warming must continue.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 13

questions.q: An inappropriate intention or action, often from lack of training or knowledge, is which error type?
questions.exp: A mistake is the wrong plan. A slip is the right plan done at the wrong time.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 21

questions.q: The correct intention carried out at the wrong time is which error type?
questions.exp: A slip is an appropriate intention or action at an inappropriate time.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 21

questions.q: A provider stays convinced the falling SpO2 is probe artifact and keeps repositioning it while the patient desaturates from a disconnect. Which error is this?
questions.exp: Failure to revise actions as conditions change ("cognitive lockup") is fixation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 21

questions.q: A provider who suspects light anesthesia looks only at the rising HR and ignores the falling BP. Which error is this?
questions.exp: Seeking data that confirm an existing hypothesis is confirmation bias.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 21

questions.q: Out of habit from the previous case, a provider pushes the routine induction sequence on a patient who was supposed to have an awake fiberoptic. Which error type fits best?
questions.exp: A correct routine (schema) fires at the wrong time, often from task overlap: capture error.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 21

questions.q: A provider believes the descending bellows will collapse with a disconnect, so she misses a disconnection. Which error type is this?
questions.exp: A faulty mental model of how the equipment works or fails is a representational error.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 21

questions.q: Misclassifying the situation, such as treating a ventilator in standby as if it were ventilating, is which error?
questions.exp: Mode error is erroneous classification of the situation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 21

questions.q: "Give the usual dose" without stating drug or amount is an example of which error?
questions.exp: Ambiguous or incomplete specification of intention is a description error.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 21

questions.q: Failing to activate the needed action, such as not starting ventilation after intubation, is which error?
questions.exp: Faulty activation: activating the wrong action or failing to activate the right one.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 21

questions.q: Automatic actions called into play by an ongoing sequence, though wrong for the situation, define which error?
questions.exp: Data-driven errors are automatic actions triggered by ongoing action sequences that don't fit.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 21

questions.q: Anesthesia simulation training was borrowed from aviation largely to combat which error?
questions.exp: Instructor note: simulation started because of tunnel vision (fixation), borrowed from pilots.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 21

questions.q: Which error types involve the provider's thinking getting stuck or biased? Select 2.
questions.exp: Fixation and confirmation bias are cognitive traps in interpreting a situation; the others are execution or communication errors.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 21

questions.q: Mishearing the surgeon and giving the wrong antibiotic is an example of which cause of error?
questions.exp: Highlighted on the slide: noise/miscommunication.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 22

questions.q: Rapid administration of vancomycin or protamine is the lecture's example of which cause of error?
questions.exp: Both drugs cause hypotension when pushed fast; not knowing this is a training gap.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 22

questions.q: A syringe swap during a critical event illustrates which cause of error?
questions.exp: Drug, syringe, or ampule swaps during crises are linked to stress.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 22

questions.q: Failing to ventilate when coming off cardiopulmonary bypass is the lecture's example of which cause?
questions.exp: High task load at bypass separation makes omissions like this more likely.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 22

questions.q: A circuit disconnects when personnel move equipment around the patient. Which cause of error is this?
questions.exp: Environmental factor: workplace constraints.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 22

questions.q: A provider misses a developing event while hand-charting vital signs. Which cause of error does the lecture assign?
c: Task complexity at a critical point
questions.exp: Doing a machine-suited task (recording) by hand diverts attention: human/machine mismatch.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 22

questions.q: The lecture's equipment-design example of error is which event?
c: A circuit disconnect when equipment is moved around the bed
The laryngoscope bulb going out during intubation
questions.exp: Instructor note: check blade lights before induction.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 22

questions.q: After disabling a noisy alarm, a provider fails to recognize a critical event. Which cause of error is this?
questions.exp: Alarms disabled because of false alarms remove a safety layer; the note says don't silence or disable alarms.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 22

questions.q: "A coherent mental model of the current state of a complex system, including prior conditions and implications for future states" defines what?
questions.exp: Highlighted on slide 23.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 23

questions.q: A state of readiness to detect and respond to changes, "sustained attention," defines what?
questions.exp: Vigilance is sustained attention to the monitored environment.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 23

questions.q: Observing one or more data streams to detect specified changes that occur at random intervals defines what?
questions.exp: Monitoring is a vigilance task focused on data streams.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 23

questions.q: Choosing between alternative diagnoses or actions based on judgments defines what?
questions.exp: Judgment forms the opinion; decision-making chooses among options based on it.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 23

questions.q: Gaining awareness or understanding through the senses defines what?
questions.exp: Perception is sensory awareness; attention is the effort to stay alert and select information.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 23

questions.q: Which are individual (human) factors known to affect vigilance? Select 3.
questions.exp: Lighting and workspace are environmental; clumsy automation is a system/equipment factor.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 24

questions.q: Which are environmental factors affecting vigilance? Select 2.
questions.exp: Environmental: noise, temperature and humidity, toxicity, lighting, workspace constraints.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 24

questions.q: Latent errors built into a system belong to which factor category?
questions.exp: System-induced (latent) errors, equipment failure, faulty mental models, and clumsy automation are system/equipment factors.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 24

questions.q: Which are stated functions of alarms? Select 3.
c: Document events for the anesthesia record
Assist when stress or workload impairs detection
Allow volumes to be turned off during stable periods
Aid a fatigued or nonvigilant provider
Replace the need for continuous provider vigilance
Detect adverse conditions in the patient or equipment
questions.exp: The lecture's three functions; alarms support vigilance, they don't replace it.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 25

questions.q: Which alarm tone does the instructor single out as very important to keep audible?
questions.exp: Note: pulse ox volume is very important; don't turn sound or volume off.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 25

questions.q: Failing to hear auditory alarms while under a high visual workload is called what?
questions.exp: Inattentional deafness reduces recognition of auditory alarms during heavy visual tasks.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 26

questions.q: How can alarms be designed so the clinician knows which alarm is sounding?
c: Varying pattern, pitch, tone, and frequency
Making all alarms the same loud tone
questions.exp: Distinct acoustic features identify the alarm and give context.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 26

questions.q: High OR noise levels can have which effect on alarms?
questions.exp: Noise can mask alarm tones.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 26

questions.q: Per the lecture, alarm limits are most useful when set so they activate when?
c: After the provider confirms the event
Only once the condition becomes critical
questions.exp: It's better to anticipate than react; limits should trigger before harm.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 27

questions.q: Which must be considered when setting an alarm limit? Select 3.
c: The cost of the monitoring equipment
The number of other alarms in the room
The rate at which the variable is changing
The response time of the measurement system
questions.exp: The five: patient condition, rate of change, measurement response time, alarm system response time, provider correction time.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 27

questions.q: A sidestream gas analyzer has a long transit time. How should that affect the alarm limit you set?
c: Disable it, because delayed data are too unreliable to use
Set it to trigger later to avoid false alarms
Set it to trigger earlier to allow for the measurement delay
No change; response time does not matter
questions.exp: Measurement response time is one of the five factors; a slower system needs a more conservative limit.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 27

questions.q: Deaths from alarms turned off after repeated false alerts led to recognition of what problem?
questions.exp: Alarm fatigue drew regulatory and policy attention.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 28

questions.q: Which strategies improve the signal-to-noise ratio of alarms? Select 3.
c: Silencing alarms whenever the patient seems stable
Reducing false-positive alerts through better design and maintenance
Raising every alarm volume to its maximum level
Secondary notification by pager or phone
Widening alarm limits so they rarely sound at all
Sound-absorbing material to lower background noise
questions.exp: The lecture lists centralizing alarms, sound absorption, device integration, visual alarms, secondary notification, and fewer false positives.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 28

questions.q: During a crisis, a provider swaps two syringes and then keeps attributing the hypotension to "light anesthesia." Which pair of error sources is present?
c: Stress-related swap followed by fixation error
Equipment design followed by mode error
Lack of training followed by capture error
questions.exp: A syringe swap in a critical situation is the stress example; refusing to revise the diagnosis is fixation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slides 21, 22

questions.q: Which term includes both awareness and judgment?
questions.exp: Cognition is the act of knowing, including awareness and judgment.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 23

questions.q: During a difficult airway, the provider stares at the video laryngoscope screen and misses the SpO2 tone dropping. Which phenomenon best explains the miss?
c: Inattentional deafness from high visual workload
Alarm fatigue from repeated false alarms earlier
questions.exp: High visual workload reduces recognition of auditory alarms.
questions.ref: Course materials: Temperature Monitoring, Vigilance, and Alarms: slide 26

questions.q: A circuit with a reservoir and partial rebreathing is classified as:
questions.exp: Semi-closed: reservoir, partial rebreathing. Closed: complete rebreathing.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 5

questions.q: A circuit with a reservoir but no rebreathing is classified as:
questions.exp: Semi-open has a reservoir and no rebreathing.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 5

questions.q: A circuit with no reservoir and no rebreathing is classified as:
questions.exp: Open: no reservoir, no rebreathing.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 5

questions.q: A circuit with a reservoir and complete rebreathing of all exhaled gas except CO2 is:
questions.exp: Closed systems rebreathe everything after CO2 is absorbed.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 5

questions.q: A circle system run at fresh gas flows well above minute ventilation, with the APL open, behaves most like which classification?
c: Open, since there is no reservoir
Closed, because the absorber is still in the circuit
questions.exp: Classification depends on reservoir and rebreathing. High enough FGF washes out exhaled gas so little is rebreathed, though the reservoir remains.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 5

questions.q: Without a CO2 absorber, roughly what fresh gas flow is enough to remove CO2 by dilution alone in an adult?
questions.exp: the lecture: FGF of 1–1.5 times minute volume removes CO2 by dilution.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 5

questions.q: Which are the ways a breathing circuit removes CO2? Select 3.
c: Valves separating exhaled from inhaled gas
Scavenger suction pulling CO2 from the inspiratory limb
questions.exp: The slide lists chemical absorption, dilution of fresh gas, and valves.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 5

questions.q: In semi-closed and closed systems, the fresh O2 and agent added must equal what?
questions.exp: Fresh gas replaces what is lost to uptake, metabolism, and leaks.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 5

questions.q: Which are desirable characteristics of a breathing circuit? Select 3.
c: CO2 removal at the rate it is produced
Slow changes in delivered gas composition
questions.exp: The six: low resistance, minimal rebreathing, CO2 removal at production rate, rapid composition changes, warm humidification, safe waste disposal.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 2

questions.q: Rebreathing in a breathing circuit helps with which function?
questions.exp: Instructor note: rebreathing helps conserve heat and humidity.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 4

questions.q: Standard corrugated breathing tubing has what bore?
questions.exp: About 1 m long with a 22 mm bore to minimize resistance.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 6

questions.q: About how much internal volume does standard breathing tubing hold per meter?
questions.exp: Internal volume is 400–500 mL per meter of length.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 6

questions.q: Resistance in standard corrugated breathing tubing is about:
questions.exp: Resistance is exceedingly small: under 1 cmH2O/L/min.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 6

questions.q: Gas flow through corrugated breathing tubing is almost always:
c: Laminar at low flow, turbulent only above 30 L/min
questions.exp: Highlighted: corrugations promote radial and longitudinal mixing, so flow is almost always turbulent.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 6

questions.q: Why don't expandable "concertina" extensions significantly add apparatus dead space?
c: They contain a one-way valve that blocks rebreathing
Their bore is larger, so gas passes faster
They add only compliant volume, not true dead space
They lie downstream of the Y-piece
questions.exp: In a circle, tubing proximal to the Y with working valves isn't dead space; extensions affect it only through compliant volume, and resistance barely changes.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 6

questions.q: Per the lecture, how is a circuit tested before use?
c: Pressurize to 75 cmH2O and hold for 1 minute
Find the O2 inflow needed to maintain 30 cmH2O in the circuit
Occlude the Y and confirm the bag empties in 5 seconds
Measure tidal volume with the ventilator off
questions.exp: Any circuit should be tested by the O2 inflow required to hold 30 cmH2O.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 6

questions.q: When does the inspiratory unidirectional valve open?
c: Only when the APL is closed
questions.exp: It opens on inspiration and closes on exhalation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 7

questions.q: What is the only critical requirement for the location of unidirectional valves in a circle?
c: One between the patient and the bag in each limb
Both must be housed inside the absorber canister
Both must be on the patient side of the Y-piece
One must sit between the APL valve and the scavenger
questions.exp: Highlighted: one valve between the patient and the bag in each limb.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 7

questions.q: In a properly working circle system, what is the only apparatus dead space?
c: The absorber canister and its housing
The full inspiratory limb from the valve onward
The entire expiratory limb back to the absorber
The distal Y-piece plus anything beyond it
questions.exp: Competent valves keep the rest of the circle out of dead space.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 7

questions.q: The expiratory valve disc sticks open. What happens?
c: The circuit becomes occluded and peak pressure rises sharply
Nothing changes, since the inspiratory valve stops rebreathing
Exhaled gas is rebreathed, raising inspired CO2
Inspired CO2 falls because more gas reaches the absorber
questions.exp: Failure to seal turns much of the circuit into dead space, causing rebreathing.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slides 7, 8

questions.q: Why must unidirectional valve discs be hydrophobic?
c: So condensation doesn’t stick them to the knife edge
So they don’t absorb volatile agent during long cases
So they repel CO2 molecules away from the valve seat
So they can be steam autoclaved between patients
questions.exp: Water would make the disc stick, increasing resistance (note: hydrophobic so they don't stick).
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 8

questions.q: The common valves in anesthesia circuits are which type?
c: Electronic solenoid valves controlled by the vent
Rubber duckbill valves that flex open
Spring-loaded ball valves seated in a cage
Dome valves with a light disk on a circular knife edge
questions.exp: Dome valves: a very light, rigid disk slightly wider than a circular knife edge.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 8

questions.q: Inspired CO2 is rising on the capnogram and the absorbent is fresh. Which machine-check item most likely failed?
questions.exp: Incompetent valves cause rebreathing even with fresh absorbent; the note says all valves must work (machine check).
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 8

questions.q: Which are functions of the reservoir bag? Select 3.
c: Visual check of ventilation and rough volume
Removal of CO2 from exhaled gas
Reservoir of gas the patient can inspire from
questions.exp: Reservoir, visual assessment, and manual ventilation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 9

questions.q: Why does a spontaneously breathing patient need a reservoir bag rather than relying on fresh gas flow?
c: The bag removes CO2 before each inspiration
Fresh gas flow pauses during each inspiratory phase
The bag warms and humidifies the inspired gas
Peak inspiratory flow exceeds fresh gas flow
questions.exp: Peak inspiratory flow during spontaneous breathing exceeds machine FGF, so a reservoir must cover the difference.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 9

questions.q: What reservoir bag size suits most adults?
questions.exp: A 3 L bag holds more than the inspiratory capacity and is easy to grasp.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 10

questions.q: How should the optimal reservoir bag volume compare with the patient's inspiratory capacity?
c: It should be half the inspiratory capacity
It should exceed the inspiratory capacity
It should equal the tidal volume
questions.exp: A deep spontaneous breath should not empty the bag.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 10

questions.q: Bag pressure-volume characteristics matter most in which situation?
c: The bag is smaller than tidal volume
The APL is left closed with gas still flowing in
The O2 flush is never used
The patient is breathing spontaneously with the APL open
questions.exp: An overfilled bag with a closed APL transmits pressure to the patient.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 10

questions.q: Where is the preferred fresh gas inflow site in a circle system?
c: Between the APL valve and the bag
Between the CO2 absorber and the inspiratory valve
Between the expiratory valve and the absorber
questions.exp: Gas enters after the absorber and before the inspiratory valve.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 11

questions.q: Tightening the APL valve during spontaneous ventilation has what effect?
questions.exp: More pressure is needed to open it, permitting PEEP during spontaneous ventilation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 11

questions.q: During spontaneous ventilation, the APL is gradually closed. What happens to rebreathing and circuit pressure?
c: Pressure rises as less gas leaves the circuit
Circuit pressure is unchanged; only scavenging changes
Circuit pressure falls; more gas leaves
questions.exp: Closing the APL holds gas in the circuit, raising pressure (PEEP) and reducing venting.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 11

questions.q: In Mapleson circuits, what does a pop-off valve do regarding rebreathing?
c: It converts the circuit to a closed system
It prevents rebreathing only during spontaneous breathing
questions.exp: Mapleson reservoirs fill with fresh and/or exhaled gas; the pop-off doesn't stop rebreathing.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 12

questions.q: Mapleson circuits use total fresh gas flows of about:
questions.exp: Gas flows totaling 1 to 2 times the minute volume.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 12

questions.q: Where is the pop-off valve most efficiently placed in a Mapleson circuit?
c: At the bag end during every mode, spontaneous or controlled
Right where fresh gas enters the circuit
Where CO2 is highest while circuit pressure is above atmospheric
Wherever CO2 concentration is lowest in the circuit
questions.exp: Highlighted: at end-exhalation during spontaneous breathing, and during inspiration with controlled breathing.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 12

questions.q: With controlled ventilation, when does the highest CO2 concentration coincide with positive circuit pressure?
questions.exp: During controlled or assisted breathing, pressure exceeds atmospheric during inspiration, so venting then removes CO2-rich gas.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 12

questions.q: Which Mapleson circuit is most efficient for spontaneous, unassisted ventilation?
questions.exp: Mapleson A (Magill, Lack, Humphrey A).
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 13

questions.q: The Bain circuit is a coaxial version of which Mapleson type?
questions.exp: Bain is a Mapleson D, efficient for controlled ventilation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 13

questions.q: Which Mapleson circuits are most efficient for assisted or controlled ventilation?
questions.exp: Mapleson D, E, F (Jackson-Rees, Bain, Humphrey DE).
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 13

questions.q: The Jackson-Rees circuit belongs to which Mapleson group?
questions.exp: Jackson-Rees is Mapleson F.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 13

questions.q: Which component do Mapleson circuits lack compared with a circle system?
questions.exp: They lack absorbers and separate limbs; CO2 is cleared by fresh gas and pop-off venting.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 13

questions.q: How do Mapleson circuits differ from a circle in their limbs?
c: One tube serves both inspiration and expiration
They have no tubing at all
They have separate inspiratory and expiratory limbs
questions.exp: They lack separate inspiratory and expiratory limbs.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 13

questions.q: On this figure, which numbered circuit is most efficient for spontaneous breathing?
questions.exp: Circuit 1 has the pop-off at the patient end and fresh gas at the bag end: Mapleson A.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 13

questions.q: Which numbered circuit corresponds to the Bain (coaxial Mapleson D) design?
questions.exp: Circuit 4 has fresh gas at the patient end and the pop-off near the bag: Mapleson D.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 13

questions.q: Which numbered circuit has no reservoir bag (a T-piece)?
questions.exp: Circuit 5 is the Mapleson E T-piece.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 13

questions.q: Which numbered circuit is the Jackson-Rees modification with an open-tailed bag?
questions.exp: Circuit 6 is Mapleson F: a T-piece with a bag at the end.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 13

questions.q: In circuit 1, where is fresh gas introduced relative to the pop-off valve?
c: At the bag end, away from the pop-off
At the patient end, next to the pop-off
questions.exp: Mapleson A has FGF at the bag end and the valve at the patient end, so exhaled alveolar gas vents efficiently during spontaneous breathing.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 13

questions.q: Which numbered circuit has the bag and pop-off together at the patient end, with no tubing between?
questions.exp: Circuit 3 is the Mapleson C (Waters-type) arrangement.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 13

questions.q: What does a heat and moisture exchanger do?
c: Adds water from a reservoir to inspired gas
Actively heats inspired gas with an electric element
Passively traps exhaled heat and moisture
questions.exp: An HME passively traps heat and moisture.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 14

questions.q: What does adding a filter to an HME (HMEF) provide?
c: Active heating of the inspired gas
questions.exp: The upper airway normally filters particles; an HMEF protects the patient from microorganisms.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 14

questions.q: Why does an ETT disrupt normal heat and moisture exchange?
c: It bypasses the upper airway, which normally conditions inspired gas
It adds water to the airway
It increases evaporation from the trachea only during exhalation
It cools inspired gas by the Venturi effect
questions.exp: Dry medical gases bypass the nose and upper airway.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 14

questions.q: By what point in the airway has most heating and humidification occurred?
questions.exp: Most heating and humidification is complete by mid-trachea.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 16

questions.q: The isothermic saturation boundary is the point where inspired gas reaches what?
questions.exp: ISB: 37°C and 100% RH, usually just below the carina.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 16

questions.q: Where does the isothermic saturation boundary normally lie?
questions.exp: It usually sits just below the carina and moves with inspired gas conditions.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 16

questions.q: Breathing dry gas through an ETT for hours moves the isothermic saturation boundary in which direction?
c: Into the upper airway above the vocal cords
Distally, exposing smaller airways to injury
questions.exp: Dry membranes humidify poorly, pushing the ISB distally.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 18

questions.q: In a normal adult, the daily net loss from airway conditioning is about:
questions.exp: About 250 mL water and 250 kcal per day.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 16

questions.q: The upper airway acts like what type of device?
c: An active heated humidifier with a water reservoir
A chemical absorber that removes inspired CO2
A one-way valve that directs gas to the alveoli
A countercurrent heat and moisture exchanger
questions.exp: It retains much of the heat and moisture it imparts, like a countercurrent HME.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 16

questions.q: Which regions do most humidification because of their mucous glands?
questions.exp: The nasopharynx, pharynx, and larynx have squamous epithelium and contribute little.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 17

questions.q: Why do the nasopharynx, pharynx, and larynx contribute little to humidification?
c: They are lined with squamous epithelium
They are lined with ciliated columnar epithelium
questions.exp: Squamous epithelium has few mucous glands; the glandular nose, trachea, and bronchi do most of the work.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 17

questions.q: Which cells form respiratory mucus in response to tracheal irritation?
questions.exp: Goblet cells secrete mucus droplets that swell and form a film around cilia.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 17

questions.q: Which are consequences of underhumidification? Select 3.
c: Viscous mucus that slows ciliary movement
Inaccurate flow sensor readings from condensation
questions.exp: The other three are consequences of OVER-humidification.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 18

questions.q: Which are consequences of overhumidification? Select 3.
c: Inaccurate volume readings from water at the flow sensors
Distal shift of the isothermic saturation boundary
questions.exp: Condensation causes these; the others result from dry gas.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 19

questions.q: Per the instructor, what helps prevent underhumidification during anesthesia?
c: High fresh gas flows of dry medical gas
Cooling inspired gas below body temperature
Removing the HME to lower airway resistance
Low flows that keep rebreathed gas warm and moist
questions.exp: Notes: low flows keep air warm and humid; high flows cool rebreathed air.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 18

questions.q: Raising fresh gas flow from 1 L/min to 8 L/min has what effect on inspired humidity and temperature?
c: Both decrease as dry fresh gas replaces rebreathed gas
Both increase, because more gas passes the absorber
questions.exp: High flows cool and dry the rebreathed gas; low flows keep it warm and humid.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 14

questions.q: HME efficiency is reduced in which situation?
c: Large tidal volumes, especially with membrane models
Use with a cuffed endotracheal tube
Small tidal volumes in adult patients
Low fresh gas flows during long maintenance phases
questions.exp: Efficiency drops with large tidal volumes.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 20

questions.q: A filter with 99.97% efficiency lets about how many test particles through per 100,000?
questions.exp: 0.03% of 100,000 is 30 particles.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 21

questions.q: Bacterial and viral filtration efficiency are tested with droplets about what size?
questions.exp: The challenge aerosol is droplets around 3.0 µm.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 21

questions.q: What is the basic principle of closed-circuit anesthesia?
c: Venting all exhaled gas to the scavenger
Adding gases at the rate the body removes them
Delivering fresh gas at twice minute ventilation
questions.exp: A constant anesthetic state is maintained by matching addition to removal.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 22

questions.q: How is the anesthetic state established before switching to closed-circuit flows?
c: Low fresh gas flow from the start
Closed circuit from induction with the vaporizer at maximum
High fresh gas flow first, then FGF lowered near steady state
questions.exp: Note: high FGF on induction, then decrease once inspired and expired concentrations match.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 22

questions.q: In a fully closed circuit, the O2 flow into the circuit equals what?
questions.exp: FGF is set equal to the uptake of each gas, including O2.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 25

questions.q: In a closed circuit, O2 administration exceeds O2 uptake. What happens to FiO2?
questions.exp: In a closed circuit, excess O2 accumulates, so inspired O2 rises; at steady state they match.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 26

questions.q: In a LOW-flow (not closed) circuit, O2 delivery slightly exceeds uptake. Why can FiO2 still fall?
c: The proportioning system lowers O2 at low flow
The vaporizer consumes O2 as it adds agent
O2 is absorbed by the CO2 absorbent granules
O2 leaves with the excess gas through the APL
questions.exp: Non-closed circuits lose gas; that gas contains O2, so delivery just above uptake may not hold FiO2.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 26

questions.q: Which are advantages of closed-circuit anesthesia? Select 3.
c: O2 consumption can be monitored by titration
No need for inspired and expired gas monitoring
Exhaled gases are already warmed and humidified
Faster changes in anesthetic depth when needed
Elimination of the CO2 absorber from the circuit
questions.exp: All three are listed advantages; closed circuits change depth slowly and require close monitoring.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 23

questions.q: Compared with a semi-closed circuit, inspired and expired gas tensions with a closed circuit are:
questions.exp: The same tensions can be established with closed, semi-closed, or open circuits.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 24

questions.q: In the low-flow example, 8 L/min with 5% isoflurane runs for 2 minutes. What is changed next?
c: Both FGF and vaporizer are turned off
The vaporizer is lowered to 1%, leaving FGF at 8 L/min
FGF is lowered to 2 L/min, leaving the vaporizer setting
questions.exp: FGF is dropped first; the vaporizer is lowered several minutes later as needed.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 27

questions.q: The low-flow example targets what expired isoflurane concentration as 1 MAC?
questions.exp: All adjustments aim for 1.1% expired isoflurane.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 27

questions.q: Which circuit is the most commonly used in the world?
c: Fully closed circuit at basal flows
Semi-closed circle with a CO2 absorber
Mapleson A with high fresh gas flow
questions.exp: The semi-closed circle with absorber.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 28

questions.q: FGF is lowered from 8 L/min to 1 L/min while keeping the same inspired agent tension. What must happen to the vaporizer setting?
questions.exp: More low-tension exhaled gas is rebreathed at low flow, so the vaporizer must go up.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 28

questions.q: Why does exhaled gas lower inspired agent tension in a semi-closed circuit?
c: Exhaled gas has higher tension than inspired gas
Exhaled gas contains no anesthetic at all
Uptake leaves exhaled gas with lower agent tension
The absorber removes anesthetic from exhaled gas
questions.exp: The patient takes up agent, so exhaled tension is lower.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 28

questions.q: Which changes speed the rise in alveolar anesthetic concentration? Select 3.
questions.exp: Note: get gas on fast by increasing MV, concentration, and FGF.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 28

questions.q: In the instructor's example, sevo is dialed so inspired is 2.3% to achieve expired 2%. Why the difference?
c: Agent is constantly taken up, so inspired must run higher
The analyzer reads inspired gas falsely high
Expired gas is diluted only by apparatus dead space
The vaporizer overdelivers at low fresh gas flow
questions.exp: In a semi-closed system you add a little more because you are constantly losing some.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 28

questions.q: Even in ideal conditions, brain anesthetic level lags end-tidal by about how long?
questions.exp: Highlighted: the brain delay is still 3 to 5 minutes.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 29

questions.q: End-tidal anesthetic concentration is used as an approximation of what?
c: Alveolar, and in turn blood, concentration
Brain concentration, with no time delay
questions.exp: End-expired approximates alveolar, which approximates blood; the brain lags.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 29

questions.q: Which are used to assess anesthetic depth? Select 3.
questions.exp: Depth integrates many signs: pupils, BP, HR, processed EEG, expired agent.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 29

questions.q: After raising the vaporizer, end-tidal agent rises quickly but the patient still moves. What best explains this?
c: Brain tension lags end-tidal by several minutes
questions.exp: Even when end-tidal equals alveolar and arterial, the brain lags 3–5 minutes.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 29

questions.q: Which machine-check finding means unidirectional valves need attention?
c: The bag fills with the APL closed
The O2 analyzer reads 21% in room air at baseline
