A valve disc fails to seat during the flow test
questions.exp: Valve competence is checked so rebreathing doesn't occur.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slides 7, 8

questions.q: A Mapleson D is used for a spontaneously breathing adult at low FGF. What happens?
c: Significant rebreathing, since D suits controlled breathing
No rebreathing, since D is efficient in every breathing mode
Barotrauma, since the pop-off sits near the bag
Hypoxia, since O2 is taken up by the absorbent
questions.exp: Mapleson D needs high FGF during spontaneous breathing; Mapleson A is the efficient spontaneous circuit.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slide 13

questions.q: Why do Mapleson circuits need higher fresh gas flows than a circle?
c: They have no absorber, so fresh gas must wash out CO2
They have higher resistance to gas flow overall
They lack a dedicated fresh gas inlet
Their reservoir bags are much smaller
questions.exp: Without chemical absorption, CO2 removal depends on dilution with fresh gas and venting.
questions.ref: Course materials: Breathing Circuits, Humidification/Filtration, and Closed Circuit: slides 5, 12

questions.q: Total response time of a gas analyzer equals what?
c: Rise time multiplied by respiratory rate
questions.exp: Transit (sample to monitor) plus rise (reaction to the change) = total response time.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 4

questions.q: The time for a gas sample to travel from the circuit to the monitor is called:
questions.exp: Transit time is sample-to-monitor travel.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 4

questions.q: The time an analyzer takes to react to a change in gas concentration is called:
questions.exp: Rise time reflects how fast the analyzer responds once the sample arrives.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 4

questions.q: Lengthening the sidestream sampling line mainly increases which component of response time?
questions.exp: A longer line adds travel time; rise time is a property of the analyzer.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slides 4, 5

questions.q: Why does the displayed EtCO2 lag behind what is happening at the airway?
c: The monitor averages 10 minutes of data
Transit and rise time delay the reading
EtCO2 is measured only during inspiration
questions.exp: Delayed response creates a lag on the monitor.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 4

questions.q: Which sampling method places the analyzer directly in the main gas stream?
questions.exp: Mainstream is non-diverting (highlighted); the sensor sits in the breathing circuit.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 6

questions.q: Mainstream analyzers are also described as:
questions.exp: Highlighted: non-diverting, since no gas is pulled away.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 6

questions.q: Which describe mainstream gas analysis? Select 3.
c: Readings affected by secretions, water vapor, and blood
Gas continuously aspirated to a remote analyzer
questions.exp: Mainstream is fast and breath-by-breath, but interfered with by secretions and less common.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 6

questions.q: Which describe sidestream sampling? Select 3.
c: Analyzer sits directly in the airway
Passes through a filter or water trap to the analyzer
Gas is continuously aspirated near the Y-piece
questions.exp: Sidestream pulls a sample to a remote analyzer, with a longer delay; high RR can reduce accuracy.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 8

questions.q: A neonate breathing at 50/min shows a low, rounded capnogram on sidestream sampling. What is the likely reason?
c: Excess dead space added by the water trap
The analyzer is reading inspired gas only
Mainstream interference from secretions in the airway
High RR exceeds the analyzer's response, lowering accuracy
questions.exp: With sidestream, fast rates can outpace transit and rise time, underreading EtCO2.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 8

questions.q: Where is a sidestream sampling adapter usually placed?
c: At the Y-piece between the circuit and the airway
In the expiratory limb next to the absorber canister
questions.exp: The adapter sits between the circuit and the patient's airway, usually at the Y.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 8

questions.q: Which law states that the total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the partial pressures?
questions.exp: Ptotal = P1 + P2 + P3; called the most important law in anesthesia.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 10

questions.q: At 760 mmHg, a gas making up 2% of a dry mixture exerts what partial pressure?
questions.exp: Dalton: 0.02 × 760 ≈ 15 mmHg.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 10

questions.q: At sea level, what is the partial pressure of 6% CO2 in dry gas?
questions.exp: 0.06 × 760 ≈ 46 mmHg. Dalton's law converts volume % to partial pressure.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 10

questions.q: Mass spectrometry can identify up to how many gases?
questions.exp: Mass spec separates ions into a spectrum, identifying up to 8 gases.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 12

questions.q: Infrared gas analysis works by measuring what?
c: Energy absorption as light passes through the sample
Ion separation in a magnetic field
Electrical current from a chemical reaction with lead
questions.exp: Infrared measures absorption to give partial pressure (dispersive vs non-dispersive).
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 12

questions.q: Which technique measures the components of a gas mixture by scattered light?
questions.exp: Raman scattering measures parts of a gas mixture.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 13

questions.q: Which gases display Raman properties and can be measured by Raman scattering? Select 3.
questions.exp: Highlighted: CO2, O2, N2, water vapor, N2O, and all volatiles display Raman properties. Monatomic noble gases do not.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 13

questions.q: Capnometry provides what?
questions.exp: Capnometry is numerical; capnography adds the waveform.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 14

questions.q: Capnometers report results at what conditions?
questions.exp: Results are reported at body temperature; water vapor can affect accuracy.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 14

questions.q: A colorimetric CO2 detector changes from purple to yellow when?
c: After about 10 minutes of continuous use
Only when CO2 is absent from the sample
During inspiration, as fresh gas arrives
During expiration, when CO2 is present
questions.exp: Purple → yellow on expiration; yellow → purple on inspiration.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 15

questions.q: After intubation, a colorimetric detector stays purple through six breaths. What does this suggest?
c: Right mainstem intubation with one-lung ventilation
No CO2; suspect esophageal tube or no lung perfusion
Correct tracheal placement with good perfusion
A normal detector reading in a ventilated patient
questions.exp: Purple means no CO2; the rapid color change is what confirms ETT placement.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 15

questions.q: A colorimetric detector cycles purple-yellow after intubation, but breath sounds are absent on the left. What is still possible?
questions.exp: Note: you can have CO2 confirmation with a right mainstem tube. CO2 confirms trachea, not depth.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 18

questions.q: Where is a colorimetric CO2 detector placed?
c: In the expiratory limb at the absorber
Between the ETT and the circuit
questions.exp: It sits between the ETT and circuit with a hydrophobic filter.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 15

questions.q: O2 analyzers measure what?
questions.exp: They measure inspired O2 fraction.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 16

questions.q: What is the overall reaction in a galvanic (fuel cell) O2 analyzer?
questions.exp: O2 reacts with the lead anode to generate current proportional to O2.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 16

questions.q: Paramagnetic O2 analyzers rely on what property of oxygen?
c: Attraction to a magnetic field from two unpaired electrons
A chemical reaction with a lead anode that makes current
High solubility in blood and tissue
High infrared absorption at specific wavelengths
questions.exp: O2 is paramagnetic because of two unpaired electrons (note: 2e⁻ in orbit).
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 17

questions.q: A paramagnetic analyzer uses two nitrogen-filled glass spheres. Why nitrogen?
c: Nitrogen absorbs infrared light at the sensor
Nitrogen reacts with lead to make a current
Nitrogen carries the paramagnetic charge itself
N2 isn’t attracted, so O2 in the field displaces them
questions.exp: O2 is drawn into the field and pushes the nonparamagnetic N2 spheres; their movement reflects O2 concentration.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 17

questions.q: What do both fuel cell and paramagnetic analyzers verify?
c: Correct ETT placement in the trachea
The patient is receiving a non-hypoxic mixture
Adequate ventilation and CO2 removal per breath
questions.exp: Note: both verify the patient is receiving a non-hypoxic mixture.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slides 16, 17

questions.q: What waveform is a mirror image of the capnogram?
questions.exp: The oxygram mirrors the capnogram.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 18

questions.q: Nitrogen monitoring can help detect which problems? Select 2.
questions.exp: Note: N2 monitoring detects leaks and VAE; it also guides preoxygenation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slides 18, 19

questions.q: Nitrogen monitoring can be used to judge the adequacy of what?
questions.exp: Washout of N2 shows denitrogenation during preoxygenation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 19

questions.q: How do MAC values of a volatile and N2O combine?
questions.exp: Volatile + N2O MAC add together.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 20

questions.q: Running high-flow O2 after turning off the vaporizer has what effect on circuit agent concentration?
questions.exp: High-flow O2 washes agent out of the circuit rapidly.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 20

questions.q: Why does the instructor favor trends over single values for ventilation parameters?
c: Trends are required by accreditation rules
Single values can’t be displayed in real time
Single values are always inaccurate on monitors
Trends reveal bronchospasm, leaks, or kinks early
questions.exp: Parameters are evaluated together, and trends catch changes earlier.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 22

questions.q: Smooth, orderly gas flow is called:
questions.exp: Laminar is smooth; turbulent is chaotic.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slides 23, 24

questions.q: Which factors convert laminar flow to turbulent? Select 3.
questions.exp: Note: vapor, mucus, narrowing, high flow, and bends/kinks cause turbulence.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 24

questions.q: Which gas property increases the tendency toward turbulent flow?
questions.exp: Turbulence rises with density and velocity; friction, viscosity, and obstruction shape also matter.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 24

questions.q: A crack in a rotameter's glass tube causes what?
c: A higher float reading with correct delivery
A leak that changes the amount delivered
questions.exp: Cracks cause leaks, changing the amount delivered.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 26

questions.q: Rotameters are which type of device?
c: Graduated glass tubes measuring gas, vapor, or liquid flow
Fuel cells measuring the O2 fraction
questions.exp: Highlighted: rotameters measure flow in a graduated glass cylinder.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 26

questions.q: A pneumotachometer measures flow from what?
c: Pressure drop as gas passes a known resistance
Rotation of a vane in the gas stream
Absorption of infrared light by the gas
Heat lost from a heated wire in the flow
questions.exp: Pressure drop across a known resistance gives flow.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 27

questions.q: Spirometry is the most common test of which part of respiratory function?
questions.exp: It assesses the ventilation portion of the respiratory system.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 28

questions.q: FEV1 is:
c: Volume forcibly exhaled in the first second
Peak flow reached during forced inspiration
Volume left in the lungs after full exhalation
Total volume exhaled after a full inhalation
questions.exp: FEV1 is the first-second forced volume; FVC is the total.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 28

questions.q: On a volume-time curve, inspiration appears as what?
questions.exp: Inspiration is the upslope, exhalation the downslope.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 30

questions.q: Volume-time curves help identify which problems? Select 3.
questions.exp: Highlighted: auto-PEEP, expiratory limb leaks, forced exhalation, and transducer miscalibration.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 30

questions.q: On these volume-time curves, which panel suggests an expiratory leak or air trapping?
questions.exp: In B, exhaled volume levels off above zero: not all the inspired volume came back.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slides 30, 31

questions.q: On these volume-time curves, which panel suggests forced exhalation or a miscalibrated flow transducer?
questions.exp: In C, the curve drops below baseline: more volume out than in.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slides 30, 31

questions.q: Which panel shows a normal volume-time curve?
questions.exp: Panel A rises during inspiration and returns cleanly to baseline.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slides 30, 31

questions.q: Which flow-time panel matches volume-controlled ventilation with constant inspiratory flow?
questions.exp: Note: flow/time is square with constant flow. Decelerating flow (B) fits pressure control.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slides 30, 32

questions.q: Which flow-time panel shows a decelerating inspiratory flow pattern?
questions.exp: Panel B's inspiratory flow peaks early and decays, typical of pressure control.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slides 30, 32

questions.q: In panel C, expiratory flow has not returned to zero when the next breath starts. What does this indicate?
questions.exp: Incomplete exhalation before the next breath means gas is trapped: auto-PEEP. Lengthen expiratory time.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 32

questions.q: How does applying PEEP change a pressure-volume loop?
c: It makes the loop show both positive and negative pressures
It shifts the loop to negative pressures
It shifts the loop so it shows only positive pressure
It has no effect on the loop
questions.exp: PEEP starts the loop above zero, so only positive pressure appears.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 33

questions.q: A spontaneously breathing patient's pressure-volume loop shows what?
questions.exp: Spontaneous breaths generate negative pressure during inspiration.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 33

questions.q: Which problems can an abnormal pressure-volume loop reveal? Select 3.
questions.exp: The slide lists compliance, equipment malfunction, and endobronchial intubation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 33

questions.q: The instructor calls which monitor the most valuable?
questions.exp: Note: capnography is the most valuable monitor.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 35

questions.q: On this capnogram, which numbered point marks where EtCO2 is measured?
questions.exp: EtCO2 is read at the end of the alveolar plateau (point 5, highlighted on the slide).
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 37

questions.q: Which numbered segment is the alveolar plateau (phase III)?
questions.exp: 1 baseline, 2 expiratory upstroke, 3 alveolar plateau, 4 inspiratory downstroke.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 37

questions.q: Segment 4 on this capnogram represents what?
questions.exp: The rapid drop as fresh gas is inhaled is the inspiratory downstroke.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 37

questions.q: Segment 1 should read what value in a normal capnogram?
questions.exp: Phase I baseline should be 0 mmHg; an elevated baseline means rebreathing.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 37

questions.q: Segment 2 becomes much less steep. What is the most likely cause?
c: Return of spontaneous breathing as paralysis fades
Expiratory airflow obstruction such as bronchospasm
questions.exp: A slanted phase II (and III) means slow, uneven emptying: the "shark fin" of obstruction.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 37

questions.q: Which capnogram panel is consistent with bronchospasm?
questions.exp: Panel A is the "shark fin": slanted upstroke and no clear plateau.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.q: Which capnogram panel shows rebreathing?
questions.exp: In C, the baseline doesn't return to zero, meaning inspired CO2 is present.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.q: Which capnogram panel shows a curare cleft?
questions.exp: A dip in the plateau when the patient breathes against the ventilator, as paralysis wears off.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.q: A patient's waveform looks like panel D. What is the best interpretation?
c: There is a large cuff leak around the ETT
Paralysis is wearing off and the patient is breathing
The CO2 absorbent is exhausted and needs changing
questions.exp: The cleft reflects spontaneous effort during a mechanical breath.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.q: A waveform changes from panel B to panel C over 30 minutes. FIRST check?
c: ETT position, looking for esophageal intubation
CO2 absorbent and unidirectional valve function
questions.exp: An elevated baseline is rebreathing: exhausted absorbent or an incompetent valve.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.q: Which capnography trend panel fits cardiac arrest?
questions.exp: A sudden drop toward zero with continued ventilation suggests loss of pulmonary blood flow.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.q: Which trend panel fits return of spontaneous circulation during CPR?
questions.exp: A sudden rise from low values signals restored pulmonary blood flow (ROSC).
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.q: Which trend panel fits hypoventilation?
questions.exp: Gradually rising EtCO2 with each breath fits hypoventilation (or rising CO2 production).
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.q: Which trend panel fits hyperventilation?
questions.exp: Gradually falling EtCO2 fits hyperventilation (or falling CO2 production).
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.q: EtCO2 drops abruptly to near zero as in panel C while airway pressures are unchanged and the circuit is intact. What should you suspect first?
c: Hyperventilation from an increase in rate
Loss of cardiac output or massive embolism
questions.exp: With an intact circuit, a sudden loss of EtCO2 means no CO2 delivery to the lungs: arrest or major PE.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.q: Why do providers hyperventilate patients with raised ICP?
c: Lower CO2 causes cerebral vasoconstriction, lowering blood flow
Lower CO2 causes cerebral vasodilation, raising blood flow
Hyperventilation raises CO2 to protect neurons
questions.exp: CO2 is a cerebral vasodilator; blowing it off constricts vessels and lowers CBF.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 36

questions.q: Why does the lecture stress EtCO2 monitoring during transport of a patient with raised ICP?
c: Transport monitors can’t display SpO2 reliably
EtCO2 replaces the need for an arterial line
CO2 swings change cerebral blood flow and ICP
questions.exp: Highlighted: increased ICP needs stable ventilation; use EtCO2 during transport.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 41

questions.q: Under normal conditions, CO2 is excreted how?
c: As fast as it is made, with no net change
Slower than it is made, so body stores rise
In bursts during the expiratory pause
Faster than it is made, so body stores fall
questions.exp: Normally excretion matches production.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 38

questions.q: Which change would raise CO2 production?
c: Increased metabolism, such as fever or MH
questions.exp: Note: things that increase metabolism increase CO2 production.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 38

questions.q: EtCO2 varies breath to breath based on which factors? Select 3.
questions.exp: The slide lists the relationship between Vt, dead space, and alveolar ventilation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 38

questions.q: What does a circuit leak do to EtCO2 accuracy?
c: Raises it falsely to arterial levels
questions.exp: Leaks make EtCO2 inaccurate.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 38

questions.q: Dead space is best described as:
questions.exp: Wasted ventilation that doesn't take part in gas exchange.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 39

questions.q: Physiologic dead space equals:
c: Alveolar dead space minus anatomic dead space
Tidal volume minus alveolar volume only at rest
Airway (anatomic) dead space plus alveolar dead space
questions.exp: Physiologic = airway + alveolar.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 39

questions.q: How does a large increase in alveolar dead space change the PaCO2-EtCO2 gradient?
c: Has no effect, since both values fall together
Reverses it, so EtCO2 exceeds PaCO2
Widens it, because EtCO2 falls while PaCO2 does not
Narrows it, because EtCO2 rises toward PaCO2
questions.exp: Unperfused alveoli add CO2-free gas, diluting EtCO2 while PaCO2 stays the same or rises.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 40

questions.q: Which cause increased dead space (V/Q mismatch) that lowers EtCO2? Select 3.
questions.exp: The slide lists hypovolemia, pulmonary hypotension, PE, nonvascular airspace, obstructed pulmonary circulation, and alveolar overdistension.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 40

questions.q: Per the instructor, capnography changes from dead space often appear when?
c: After SpO2 has started to fall
questions.exp: Note: EtCO2 often changes before hemodynamic changes appear.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 40

questions.q: During CPR, what PETCO2 indicates sufficient pulmonary blood flow from compressions?
questions.exp: 10 mmHg achieves sufficient pulmonary blood flow; low values suggest poor compressions.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 41

questions.q: During CPR, PETCO2 is 6 mmHg. What is the best response?
questions.exp: Below 10 mmHg suggests inadequate compressions; fix depth, rate, and recoil.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 41

questions.q: Why is pulmonary embolism hard to diagnose with capnography alone?
c: Capnography can’t reflect dead space changes
PE has no effect on CO2 elimination
Baseline alveolar dead space is usually unknown
questions.exp: Without a known baseline, a drop is hard to attribute.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 42

questions.q: During sedation cases, capnography helps detect what?
questions.exp: It shows obstruction, though direct observation is just as important.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 42

questions.q: Functional saturation (SaO2) is calculated as:
questions.exp: Highlighted: functional saturation uses only O2Hb and reduced Hb.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 44

questions.q: Why does fractional saturation read lower than functional saturation with significant carbon monoxide?
c: Functional saturation counts COHb as oxygenated
The two values are identical in CO poisoning
Fractional includes COHb and MetHb in the denominator
questions.exp: Fractional = O2Hb / (O2Hb + RHb + COHb + MetHb); dyshemoglobins enlarge the denominator.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 44

questions.q: In CaO2 = 1.34 × Hb × SaO2 + 0.003 × PaO2, what does 0.003 × PaO2 represent?
questions.exp: The first term is Hb-bound O2; the second is dissolved O2.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 44

questions.q: Hb 10 g/dL, SaO2 100%, PaO2 100 mmHg. What is CaO2?
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 44

questions.q: Oxygen delivery to tissues depends on CaO2 and what?
questions.exp: DO2 = CaO2 × CO (the slide writes "+", but delivery is the product).
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 44

questions.q: How many O2 binding sites does each hemoglobin molecule have?
questions.exp: Each Hb carries up to four O2 molecules.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 45

questions.q: The Beer-Lambert law is written as:
questions.exp: A = absorbance, ε = molar absorption coefficient, c = concentration, l = path length.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slides 47, 48

questions.q: In the Beer-Lambert law, what does "l" stand for?
questions.exp: l is the distance light travels through the sample.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 48

questions.q: Per Beer-Lambert, doubling the concentration of an absorber while holding path length constant does what to absorbance?
questions.exp: Absorbance is directly proportional to concentration.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 48

questions.q: Which device relies on the Beer-Lambert law?
questions.exp: Pulse oximetry analyzes light absorbed through tissue.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 48

questions.q: Fetal hemoglobin has what effect on pulse oximetry?
questions.exp: HbF: no effect (note: HgF okay).
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 50

questions.q: Which can cause pulse oximetry errors? Select 3.
questions.exp: Also low perfusion and temperature; HbF has no effect.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 50

questions.q: Dyshemoglobins such as methemoglobin cause errors because they:
c: They increase perfusion at the probe site
Cannot carry O2 but still absorb light
They carry O2 more efficiently than normal Hb
They are invisible to the oximeter’s light
questions.exp: They can't carry O2 yet change light absorption, misleading the oximeter.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 50

questions.q: Per the instructor, which finger has the most perfusion for probe placement?
questions.exp: Note: middle finger has the most perfusion.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 50

questions.q: How do modern oximeters reduce motion artifact?
c: Longer signal averaging and ECG synchronization
Using a single wavelength of light
Increasing the light intensity at the probe site
questions.exp: The slide lists increased signal time and ECG synchronization.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 51

questions.q: SpO2 is determined from which signal?
questions.exp: Highlighted: total − noise = noise-free signal used for SpO2.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 51

questions.q: A dependent probe position can lower SpO2 by up to how much?
questions.exp: The slide lists up to 8%.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 51

questions.q: A patient on 100% O2 has PaO2 falling from 450 to 150 mmHg, but SpO2 stays 100%. What limitation does this show?
c: SpO2 gives no early warning of falling PaO2
The probe is malpositioned on the finger
Pulse oximetry overestimates PaO2 at all levels
questions.exp: On the flat part of the curve, large PaO2 drops don't change saturation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 52

questions.q: Pulse oximetry became standard of care in what year?
questions.exp: Standard of care since 1986.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 53

questions.q: Where is hypoxemia more common?
c: Neither; hypoxemia is rare after surgery
questions.exp: Hypoxemia in PACU exceeds the OR; transport without O2 contributes.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slides 53, 54

questions.q: Which patient factors are associated with postoperative desaturation? Select 3.
questions.exp: Also poor physical status.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 54

questions.q: Which situation is a classic setup for postoperative desaturation?
c: Supine position with O2 by mask
Arrival in PACU on a nonrebreather
Transport to PACU without supplemental O2
questions.exp: SpO2 falls during transport without supplemental O2.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 53

questions.q: Peak pressure rises suddenly with a shark-fin capnogram. Which cause fits both?
questions.exp: Bronchospasm raises airway resistance and slows exhalation; a disconnect or leak lowers pressure.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 22

questions.q: Airway pressure and EtCO2 both fall to near zero suddenly. Most likely cause?
questions.exp: Loss of pressure and CO2 together point to a disconnect; obstruction raises pressure.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 22

questions.q: Infrared analyzers are categorized as which two types?
questions.exp: The slide lists dispersive vs non-dispersive infrared.
questions.ref: Course materials: Franck, Respiratory Monitoring: slide 12

questions.q: The process of eliminating CO2 is called:
questions.exp: Ventilation removes CO2; oxygenation is O2 intake.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 3, 68

questions.q: Gas solubility in a liquid is directly proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid. This is:
questions.exp: Henry's law governs solubility; Dalton's governs partial pressures in a mixture.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 3, 68

questions.q: How does systemic vascular tone respond to low O2 or high CO2?
questions.exp: Systemic vessels dilate with hypoxia or hypercarbia (the pulmonary circulation constricts).
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 4, 69

questions.q: Filling the lungs with O2 so tissues are supplied without ventilation is called:
questions.exp: Apneic oxygenation uses the pulmonary O2 reservoir without breathing.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 4, 69

questions.q: During spontaneous inspiration, diaphragm contraction makes intrathoracic pressure:
questions.exp: Negative pressure draws gas in; mechanical ventilation uses positive pressure instead.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 5, 70

questions.q: Change in lung volume per change in pressure is called:
questions.exp: Compliance = ΔV/ΔP.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 6, 71

questions.q: Pulmonary fibrosis has what effect on compliance?
c: Increases it only at high volumes
questions.exp: Stiff lungs need more pressure for the same volume.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 6, 71

questions.q: Bronchoconstriction or ETT obstruction has what effect on resistance?
questions.exp: Narrower conduits raise the pressure needed for a given flow.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 6, 71

questions.q: Volume equals:
questions.exp: Flow = volume/time, so volume = flow × time; pressure = flow × resistance.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 7, 72

questions.q: Flow multiplied by resistance gives:
questions.exp: P = flow × R.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 7, 72

questions.q: Airway pressure equals:
questions.exp: Airway pressure adds the resistive term to alveolar pressure.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 8, 73

questions.q: Alveolar pressure equals:
questions.exp: No resistive term because there is no flow at the alveolus at end-inspiration.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 8, 73

questions.q: A patient develops bronchospasm during volume control. Which term of the airway pressure equation rises?
questions.exp: Bronchospasm raises resistance, increasing the resistive component (PIP) while alveolar pressure changes less.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 8

questions.q: Pneumoperitoneum is established during volume control. Which term of the airway pressure equation rises most?
questions.exp: Insufflation reduces respiratory system compliance, raising the elastic term and plateau pressure.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 8

questions.q: Which are the four main components of a mechanical ventilator? Select 3.
questions.exp: The four: power source, controls, monitors, safety features.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 11

questions.q: A piston ventilator's drive force comes from:
questions.exp: Pistons are electric; bellows are driven by compressed gas.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 15

questions.q: A bellows ventilator's drive force comes from:
c: An electric motor moving a piston
Compressed driving gas squeezing the bellows
questions.exp: Pneumatic bellows use driving gas.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 15

questions.q: Ascending bellows rise during which phase?
questions.exp: Ascending bellows "stand," rising during expiration.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 16

questions.q: What happens to ascending bellows with a circuit disconnection?
c: They rise normally from room air entrainment
They fail to rise fully or collapse
They lock in the inspiratory position
questions.exp: Ascending bellows can't refill without exhaled gas, making a disconnect visible.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 16

questions.q: What happens to descending bellows with a circuit disconnection?
c: They rise to the top of the housing
They stop moving and lock in place
They still fill with room air and look normal
They collapse immediately and stay down
questions.exp: Descending bellows hang by gravity and entrain air, hiding the disconnect.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 17

questions.q: Why are ascending bellows considered safer for detecting disconnection?
c: They have a higher relief valve opening pressure
They entrain room air during a disconnect
They use an electric motor as the drive
Ascending bellows need exhaled gas to rise
questions.exp: A disconnected circuit means the bellows don't refill, an obvious visual sign.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 16, 17

questions.q: The ascending bellows spill (relief) valve opens at about what pressure?
questions.exp: The spill valve opens at about 2–4 cmH2O, allowing scavenging during expiration.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 16

questions.q: What side effect does the ascending bellows spill valve produce?
c: A small amount of baseline PEEP
questions.exp: Note: the spill valve adds some PEEP.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 16

questions.q: Which safety features help detect disconnection with descending bellows on newer machines? Select 3.
c: Sensors detecting failure to return to full hang
A spill valve opening at 75 cmH2O
questions.exp: Because descending bellows can look normal, alarms and sensors are needed.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 17

questions.q: Which are consequences of a hole in the bellows? Select 3.
c: Altered FiO2 depending on drive gas
Lower airway pressure at the patient
questions.exp: A leak exposes the circuit to drive gas: barotrauma, FiO2 changes, and agent dilution.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 18

questions.q: A bellows leak develops on a machine using 100% O2 as drive gas. How does FiO2 change?
c: It falls only if N2O is in use
questions.exp: O2 drive gas leaking into the circuit enriches the inspired O2.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 18

questions.q: A bellows leak develops on a machine using an air/O2 drive gas while delivering 100% O2. How does FiO2 change?
questions.exp: Air in the drive gas dilutes the O2 in the circuit.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 18

questions.q: Expired agent drops unexpectedly with ascending bellows and normal vaporizer function. Which equipment problem fits?
c: Bellows leak releasing agent on expiration
questions.exp: In ascending bellows, a leak lets agent escape on expiration, diluting the anesthetic.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 18

questions.q: Which ventilator does NOT need driving gas?
c: Pneumatic bellows with an air drive
questions.exp: Notes: piston: don't need drive gas, rigid, needs pop-off.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 19

questions.q: During an O2 pipeline failure with only a cylinder available, which ventilator type conserves O2 best?
c: Any bellows ventilator with high FGF
Piston, since it needs no driving gas
questions.exp: The piston is useful during pipeline failure because it doesn't consume O2 as drive gas.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 19, 22

questions.q: A piston ventilator's positive pressure relief valve opens at:
questions.exp: Positive relief at 75 cmH2O; negative at −8.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 20

questions.q: A piston ventilator's negative pressure relief valve opens at:
questions.exp: It opens at −8 cmH2O, giving some protection against NEEP.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 20

questions.q: A piston's negative pressure relief valve opens repeatedly during a case with low FGF. What is the main risk?
c: Room air entrainment dilutes agent, risking awareness
Rising agent concentration in the circuit
questions.exp: Note: negative will dilute → awareness.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 20

questions.q: Negative end-expiratory pressure (NEEP) is a recognized risk of which ventilator?
questions.exp: Piston disadvantages include potential for NEEP.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 20, 22

questions.q: Fresh gas decoupling is a feature of which ventilator type?
questions.exp: Board topic: piston ventilators use fresh gas decoupling.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 21

questions.q: During inspiration with fresh gas decoupling, where does fresh gas go?
questions.exp: The decoupling valve closes and FGF accumulates in the bag.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 21

questions.q: During expiration with fresh gas decoupling, where does fresh gas go?
c: Out to the scavenger through the APL
Into the reservoir bag, bypassing the piston
Into the piston to fill it for the next breath
questions.exp: The valve opens and FGF fills the piston.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 21

questions.q: With fresh gas decoupling, raising FGF from 2 to 8 L/min changes delivered tidal volume how?
c: It increases with the extra flow
It decreases as gas is vented
questions.exp: Board topic and note: decoupling means FGF does not add to Vt.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 21

questions.q: Without fresh gas decoupling, raising FGF during volume control has what effect on delivered tidal volume?
c: It has no effect on delivered volume
It decreases only at high respiratory rates
It increases, because fresh gas adds to each breath
It decreases, because the extra fresh gas is vented
questions.exp: Without decoupling, FGF during inspiration adds to the set volume.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 21

questions.q: Which are benefits of fresh gas decoupling? Select 2.
c: Higher delivered Vt at high FGF
questions.exp: It isolates FGF from the circuit during inspiration, keeping Vt consistent.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 21

questions.q: In a decoupled piston circuit, the reservoir bag inflates and deflates with each breath during mechanical ventilation. What does this reflect?
c: The APL valve is stuck in the closed position
The decoupling valve has failed in the open position
Normal function of a decoupled piston system
A disconnection at the Y-piece is present
questions.exp: The bag acts as the fresh gas reservoir in decoupled systems.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 21

questions.q: Which is an advantage of a piston ventilator?
c: It adapts easily to non-rebreathing circuits
It is loud, so cycling is easy to hear
It adds no PEEP to the system
questions.exp: Advantages: no PEEP, precise Vt, compliance/leak compensation, decoupling, useful in pipeline failure.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 22

questions.q: Which are disadvantages of piston ventilators? Select 3.
c: Adds a baseline PEEP to the system
Requires O2 as its driving gas
Quiet, so cycling may not be heard
Not easily adapted to non-rebreathing circuits
questions.exp: The piston adds no PEEP, gives precise volumes, and needs no driving gas.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 22

questions.q: Why do piston ventilators deliver more precise tidal volumes?
c: Compliance/leak compensation and fresh gas decoupling
Absence of a reservoir bag anywhere in the circuit
A spill valve that adds a little PEEP
Higher driving gas pressure in the housing
questions.exp: The slide lists compliance and leak compensation and fresh gas decoupling.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 22

questions.q: A turbine ventilator raises circuit pressure during inspiration by doing what?
c: Opening a solenoid to the pipeline
Moving a piston with a motor
questions.exp: Higher revolutions produce higher circuit pressures.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 23

questions.q: Which are listed benefits of turbine ventilators? Select 2.
c: Built-in negative pressure protection at −8 cmH2O
Added PEEP from a spill valve
Use of O2 as drive gas
questions.exp: Turbines reduce dead space and improve mixing and gas concentrations.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 23

questions.q: Solenoid valves control gas flow by:
c: A bimetallic strip that bends with heat
A float rising in a tapered tube
Pneumatic pressure from the pipeline only
An electric current creating a magnetic field
questions.exp: Solenoids precisely control air and O2, Vt timing, and pressure.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 24

questions.q: Which cycling mechanism do most anesthesia ventilators use in controlled modes?
questions.exp: Note: time-cycled is the majority of vents.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 25

questions.q: In time-cycled ventilation, what ends inspiration?
c: Flow falling to a preset value
questions.exp: Set RR and I:E determine timing.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 25

questions.q: Which is a drawback of time-cycled controlled ventilation?
c: Ventilation stops with low respiratory drive
questions.exp: Ventilation is unaffected by compliance or drive, which risks dyssynchrony with patient effort.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 25

questions.q: In flow-cycled ventilation, inspiration ends when:
c: Flow drops to a preset value
questions.exp: Flow-cycled ends at a preset flow (L/min or % of peak).
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 26

questions.q: Per the instructor, flow cycling is typically set to end inspiration at about what percent of peak flow?
questions.exp: Note: set to stop I at about 20%, then switch to E.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 26

questions.q: How does poor compliance affect tidal volume in flow-cycled modes?
questions.exp: Poor compliance means flow decays faster, cycling earlier with less volume.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 26

questions.q: In older volume-cycled ventilators, what varies with compliance and resistance?
questions.exp: Volume is fixed; pressure and flow vary, with a higher pneumothorax risk.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 27

questions.q: Older pressure-cycled ventilators have what drawback with poor compliance?
c: Increased pneumothorax risk from fixed volume
questions.exp: Inspiration ends at the preset pressure, so stiff lungs get less volume.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 27

questions.q: Per the instructor, what FiO2 is typical during maintenance?
questions.exp: Note: maintenance 30–50%; high fractions for preox, induction, emergence.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 31

questions.q: Why use a low FiO2 during maintenance?
c: Reduce airway fire risk and O2 toxicity
questions.exp: Low fractions are used for fire risk and maintenance; avoid toxicity and hypoxic mixes.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 31

questions.q: When are high FiO2 values appropriate? Select 2.
c: Routine maintenance of a healthy patient
questions.exp: High fractions for preoxygenation, induction, and emergence; low for fire risk and maintenance.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 31

questions.q: To maintain EtCO2 of about 30–40 mmHg in a typical adult, the lecture suggests what RR?
questions.exp: RR 10–16 for EtCO2 about 30–40.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 32

questions.q: Per the instructor, EtCO2 typically runs how much below PaCO2?
questions.exp: Note: gradient 2–5 mmHg, ETCO2 lower.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 32

questions.q: Near emergence, why might you lower the ventilator rate?
c: Allow CO2 to rise and stimulate respiratory drive
Lower CO2 to deepen the anesthetic before waking
questions.exp: Note: on emergence ↓RR → ↑CO2 → ↑respiratory drive.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 32

questions.q: When low tidal volume ventilation is used, what often must change to manage CO2?
questions.exp: Lower Vt may need higher rates to maintain minute ventilation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 32

questions.q: Laparoscopic CO2 insufflation tends to do what to EtCO2 at constant ventilation?
questions.exp: Absorbed CO2 raises EtCO2; increase minute ventilation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 32

questions.q: Lengthening inspiratory time (increasing the I:E ratio) mainly improves what?
c: CO2 clearance from the alveoli each breath
questions.exp: Longer inspiration recruits alveoli; note: ↑I → ↑oxygenation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 33

questions.q: Which are effects of lengthening inspiratory time? Select 3.
questions.exp: Note: ↑I → ↑oxygenation but ↓venous return, SV, BP.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 33

questions.q: Lengthening expiratory time (decreasing the I:E ratio) mainly improves what?
c: CO2 clearance and less air trapping
questions.exp: Note: ↑E → ↑ventilation; good for COPD.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 34

questions.q: A COPD patient shows rising peak pressures and expiratory flow that doesn't reach zero. Best I:E change?
questions.exp: Obstructive disease needs more time to empty; auto-PEEP improves with longer expiration.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 34

questions.q: The default I:E ratio for mechanical ventilation is:
questions.exp: Default 1:2; normal spontaneous 1:2–1:4.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 35

questions.q: Which I:E range suits obstructive lung disease?
questions.exp: Obstructive disease: 1:3–1:4 (note: 1:3–5).
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 35

questions.q: Which I:E range is listed for ARDS?
questions.exp: ARDS can need longer inspiration, up to inverse ratio.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 35

questions.q: Increasing inspiratory flow rate while keeping RR and Vt constant has what effect?
c: Shortens inspiratory time and lengthens expiratory time
Lengthens both inspiratory and expiratory time
Leaves inspiratory and expiratory time unchanged
Lengthens inspiratory time and shortens expiration
questions.exp: Faster flow delivers the volume sooner, leaving more time to exhale.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 35

questions.q: An inspiratory pause (plateau) is thought to improve what?
questions.exp: A no-flow period during inspiration is thought to improve oxygenation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 33

questions.q: The recommended tidal volume is about:
questions.exp: 6–8 mL/kg IBW (note: 7 mL/kg).
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 36

questions.q: Tidal volume should be calculated from which weight?
c: Adjusted body weight for all patients
questions.exp: Lung size follows height, not total weight.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 36

questions.q: Set Vt 500 mL, circuit compliance 4 mL/cmH2O, PIP 25 cmH2O. Using the lecture formula, about what Vt is delivered?
questions.exp: Delivered Vt = set Vt − (compliance × PIP) = 500 − 100 = 400 mL.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 36

questions.q: Circuit compliance stays the same but PIP doubles. How does the volume lost to the circuit change?
questions.exp: Volume lost = circuit compliance × PIP, so it scales with pressure.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 36

questions.q: Which are suggested benefits of low tidal volume ventilation? Select 3.
c: Higher EtCO2 at the same rate is desirable
Lower risk of atelectasis without PEEP
questions.exp: Listed benefits; low Vt often needs a higher RR and PEEP.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 36

questions.q: Which trigger method do anesthesia ventilators typically use?
questions.exp: Note: anesthesia uses flow trigger, usually 2 L/min; flow is most sensitive.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 37

questions.q: Which trigger type is most sensitive?
questions.exp: Note: flow is most sensitive.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 37

questions.q: Trigger sensitivity is set too high (very hard to trigger). What happens?
c: The patient's work of breathing increases
The patient’s work of breathing decreases
PEEP is lost from the circuit
questions.exp: Low sensitivity makes the patient work harder to start a breath.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 37

questions.q: Trigger sensitivity is set too low (very easy to trigger). What happens?
c: The patient must work harder to start each breath
The ventilator may trigger without a true patient effort
Triggered breaths fail to be delivered
questions.exp: Highly sensitive settings can auto-trigger from noise or leaks.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 37

questions.q: A pressure trigger example in the lecture is about:
questions.exp: Pressure trigger: negative inspiratory pressure, such as −3 cmH2O.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 37

questions.q: The default PEEP is:
questions.exp: Default 5 cmH2O, titrated to SpO2.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 38

questions.q: When titrating PEEP, the lecture suggests increasing by about:
questions.exp: Increase about 2 cmH2O every 10–15 minutes to 8–10.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 38

questions.q: Which are risks of high PEEP? Select 3.
questions.exp: Note: can ↑ICP, hypotension, ↓venous return, barotrauma.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 38

questions.q: What is the main purpose of PEEP?
c: Shorten expiratory time to clear CO2
Prevent alveolar collapse and improve oxygenation
Increase CO2 elimination from the alveoli
questions.exp: PEEP keeps alveoli open at end-exhalation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 38

questions.q: What is the PIP goal in the lecture?
questions.exp: Goal under 35–40; note: 40 is the default maximum.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 39

questions.q: Per the instructor, a typical PIP for a healthy patient is about:
questions.exp: Note: normal 13–20; sick or obese about 30.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 39

questions.q: Which cause increased PIP through increased airway resistance? Select 3.
questions.exp: Pneumoperitoneum, Trendelenburg, and pneumothorax lower compliance.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 40

questions.q: Which cause increased PIP through decreased lung compliance? Select 3.
questions.exp: Kinks, secretions, and bronchospasm raise resistance.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 40

questions.q: Which cause PIP to decrease? Select 3.
questions.exp: Lower PIP comes from less resistance, better compliance, a leak, or switching to pressure control.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 41

questions.q: PIP suddenly drops from 22 to 8 cmH2O during volume control, and exhaled Vt falls. FIRST action?
c: Check for a disconnection or leak
questions.exp: A sudden pressure drop with lower exhaled volume points to a leak or disconnect.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 41

questions.q: Switching from volume control to pressure control usually has what effect on displayed PIP?
questions.exp: Switching to pressure control is listed among causes of lower PIP.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 41

questions.q: During a laparoscopic case, PIP climbs to 38 cmH2O after insufflation. Per the instructor, what is a reasonable step?
c: Ignore it; PIP below 40 is always acceptable
Disconnect the circuit to relieve pressure
Disconnect the circuit briefly to relieve pressure
Discuss lowering insufflation pressure with the surgeon
questions.exp: Note: potential for releasing some insufflation; talk to the surgeon.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 39, 41

questions.q: Plateau pressure is measured when?
questions.exp: Note: pressure in the circuit when there's no airflow, right before expiration.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 42

questions.q: Plateau pressure best reflects what?
questions.exp: With no flow, the resistive component drops out.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 42

questions.q: Static compliance is calculated as:
questions.exp: Highlighted red on the slide.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 42

questions.q: Dynamic compliance is calculated as:
questions.exp: Note: dynamic = Vt / (PIP − PEEP).
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 42

questions.q: Vt 500 mL, Pplat 25 cmH2O, PEEP 5 cmH2O. Static compliance?
questions.exp: 500 / (25 − 5) = 25 mL/cmH2O. 20 uses Pplat alone; 16.7 uses Pplat + PEEP.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 42

questions.q: Vt 600 mL, PIP 35, Pplat 20, PEEP 5 cmH2O. Dynamic compliance?
questions.exp: 600 / (35 − 5) = 20. Using Pplat gives 40 (static).
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 42

questions.q: Driving pressure equals:
questions.exp: Driving pressure (Pplat − PEEP) reflects stress on the lung.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 43

questions.q: Which strategy keeps plateau pressure low to reduce ventilator-induced lung injury?
c: Higher tidal volume with zero PEEP
Lower tidal volume with reasonable PEEP
questions.exp: Lower Vt and reasonable PEEP limit overdistension.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 42, 43

questions.q: On this pressure-time waveform, which numbered point is the plateau pressure?
questions.exp: 1 is PIP, 2 is Pplat (inspiratory hold, no flow), 3 is PEEP.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 42, 43

questions.q: On this waveform, the difference between points 1 and 2 reflects what?
c: The PEEP level set on the vent
A leak in the circuit or cuff
questions.exp: PIP minus Pplat is the resistive pressure; Pplat minus PEEP is the elastic (driving) pressure.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 42, 43

questions.q: On this waveform, which pair of points gives driving pressure?
questions.exp: Driving pressure = Pplat (2) − PEEP (3).
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 42, 43

questions.q: Compared with the gray baseline, which panel shows a resistance problem?
questions.exp: High peak with unchanged plateau means more resistive pressure: bronchospasm, kink, secretions.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 43

questions.q: Which panel shows a compliance problem?
questions.exp: Peak and plateau both rise: the lungs or chest wall are stiffer (insufflation, Trendelenburg, atelectasis).
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 43

questions.q: Which panel shows an elevated baseline (PEEP) problem?
questions.exp: The entire waveform sits higher, starting from a raised baseline: PEEP or auto-PEEP.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 43

questions.q: A patient's waveform changes from baseline to panel A. Which is the most likely cause?
questions.exp: Panel A is a resistance pattern; the others lower compliance (panel B pattern).
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 43

questions.q: In controlled (mandatory) ventilation, who triggers and cycles the breath?
c: The machine triggers and the patient cycles
The patient triggers and the machine cycles
questions.exp: Controlled: machine triggered and cycled; the vent does all the work.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 44, 45

questions.q: In an assisted breath, who triggers and who cycles?
questions.exp: Assisted: patient-triggered, machine-cycled.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 44

questions.q: Controlled modes are necessary for which patients?
c: Patients with an LMA breathing spontaneously
Patients with neuromuscular weakness who breathe well
questions.exp: Patient effort doesn't influence controlled breaths, so they suit apneic patients.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 45

questions.q: In volume control ventilation, which parameter is fixed?
questions.exp: Volume is fixed; PIP varies.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 46

questions.q: In volume control, what happens to PIP when compliance decreases?
questions.exp: Fixed volume into stiffer lungs needs more pressure.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 46

questions.q: Which risk is associated with each mode in the lecture?
questions.exp: VCV fixes volume so pressure can climb; PCV fixes pressure so volume can swing.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 46, 48

questions.q: In pressure control ventilation, which parameter is fixed?
questions.exp: Pressure is fixed; Vt and flow vary.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 48

questions.q: During pressure control, the surgeon releases the pneumoperitoneum. What happens to tidal volume?
questions.exp: Better compliance at the same pressure delivers more volume; watch for volutrauma (note).
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 48

questions.q: During pressure control, bronchospasm develops. What happens to tidal volume?
questions.exp: Higher resistance at fixed pressure means less volume and possible hypoventilation.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 48

questions.q: Which inspiratory flow pattern is typical of pressure control?
questions.exp: PCV delivers high initial flow that decays; VCV uses constant square flow.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 47, 49

questions.q: PCV-VG adjusts what to maintain the set tidal volume?
questions.exp: Pressure changes breath to breath based on compliance.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 50

questions.q: Why does PCV-VG still require vigilance over PIP alarms?
c: It works only during spontaneous breathing
Pressure rises automatically to hold the set Vt
It can’t change inspiratory pressure at all
It turns off the pressure alarms by design
questions.exp: The algorithm raises pressure to maintain volume, so pressures can creep up.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 50

questions.q: What problem with plain PCV does PCV-VG address?
c: Inability to set PEEP in pressure modes
Lack of a backup rate during apnea
Large Vt swings with sudden compliance changes
High peak pressures caused by a fixed volume
questions.exp: PCV-VG promotes constant ventilation despite patient or surgical changes.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 50

questions.q: Which situations favor pressure control? Select 3.
c: Need for a guaranteed fixed volume regardless of compliance
Cuffed ETT with high compliance and no leak concerns
Normal lungs in a short supine case only
questions.exp: Low compliance, high-pressure risks, uncuffed tubes, and LMAs favor PCV.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 51

questions.q: Per the instructor, what pressure limit is used with PCV through an LMA?
questions.exp: Note: LMA doesn't want high pressure; PCV ≤ about 20.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 51

questions.q: In assist-control ventilation, what does a spontaneous patient-triggered breath receive?
c: Half of the preset tidal volume
Pressure support only, no set volume
questions.exp: Every triggered breath gets the full set Vt.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 52

questions.q: In assist-control, the patient breathes faster than the set rate. What happens?
c: The ventilator stops assisting those breaths
Controlled breaths are added on top of the assisted ones
Tidal volume is reduced to compensate
No controlled breaths are given; all breaths are assisted
questions.exp: Spontaneous effort over the set RR means all breaths are patient-triggered.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 52

questions.q: In SIMV, what happens if no patient effort is detected within the timing window?
c: The ventilator alarms and stops cycling
No breath is delivered during that interval
A mandatory breath at the start of the interval
questions.exp: No change: mandatory breath at the beginning of the interval.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 54

questions.q: In SIMV, effort is detected within the timing window. When is the mandatory breath delivered?
c: It is skipped for that cycle
Immediately after the next spontaneous breath ends
In sync with the effort, at the end of the interval
questions.exp: The mandatory breath is synchronized with the detected effort.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 54

questions.q: Which are benefits of SIMV? Select 3.
c: Delivers full Vt with every spontaneous breath
Pressure support available for spontaneous breaths
Eliminates the need for a backup rate
questions.exp: Note: helps ↓barotrauma, prevents breath stacking.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 56

questions.q: Why is SIMV less likely than assist-control to cause breath stacking?
c: It uses a faster inspiratory flow rate
It delivers smaller mandatory breaths each cycle
It lengthens inspiratory time on each breath
It delivers breaths only when the airway is nearly empty
questions.exp: Synchronizing breaths to the sensed volume prevents stacking.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 56

questions.q: What does pressure support do?
c: Adds a preset pressure to patient-triggered breaths
Delivers a fixed volume at a set rate
Holds one continuous pressure throughout the cycle
questions.exp: PSV supports spontaneous breaths with a preset pressure.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 57

questions.q: What does PSV-Pro add to standard PSV?
c: Backup machine breaths during apnea or failed triggers
A higher ceiling on pressure support levels
A guaranteed tidal volume on every single breath
questions.exp: PSV-Pro switches between PCV and PSV as needed.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 57

questions.q: The pressure support range listed in the lecture is:
questions.exp: Goal 5–20 cmH2O.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 57

questions.q: A pressure-supported breath typically cycles to exhalation when flow falls to about what fraction of peak?
questions.exp: The PSV graph shows cycling off at about 25% of peak flow.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slides 57, 58

questions.q: A patient on PSV with an LMA becomes apneic after an opioid bolus. Which mode prevents a gap in ventilation?
c: Spontaneous mode with the APL open
questions.exp: PSV-Pro delivers backup breaths in apnea; standard PSV needs patient triggers (note: babysit PSV, watch MV).
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 57

questions.q: In spontaneous mode, partially closing the APL valve does what?
questions.exp: Note: spontaneous = open APL; partial closure = some PEEP.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 59

questions.q: BiPAP differs from CPAP by providing what?
c: A fixed tidal volume with each breath
Two pressure levels, inspiratory and expiratory
questions.exp: BiPAP has P1 (inspiratory) and P2 (expiratory); CPAP has one level.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 60

questions.q: High-frequency ventilation delivers more than how many breaths per minute?
questions.exp: HFV: greater than 150 cycles/min with low Vt.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 62

questions.q: APRV is mainly used for which condition?
questions.exp: APRV holds high CPAP for recruitment with brief releases; note: risk of barotrauma and air trapping.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 62

questions.q: What are goals of a recruitment maneuver? Select 2.
questions.exp: Goals: reverse atelectasis, improve oxygenation and shunt, possibly better compliance and lower driving pressure.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 63

questions.q: A typical manual recruitment maneuver uses what pressure and duration?
questions.exp: "30 for 30": about 30–40 cmH2O, held more than 10 seconds.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 64

questions.q: Recruitment maneuvers should be avoided in which patient?
c: Healthy patient with atelectasis after induction
questions.exp: Avoid in neurotrauma and pneumothorax; also watch for hypotension.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 64

questions.q: Right after a successful manual recruitment, the patient is switched back to the ventilator with zero PEEP. What is the main concern?
questions.exp: Recruited areas can be lost when switching from bag to vent; maintain PEEP.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 64

questions.q: Per the instructor, how is a manual recruitment maneuver done?
c: Open the APL fully and release the bag quickly
Close the APL halfway; squeeze the bag ≥10 s to a PIP near 40
Raise RR to 30 breaths/min for one full minute
Press the O2 flush for 10 seconds straight
questions.exp: Note: close APL ½ way, squeeze reservoir bag ≥10 sec, PIP about 40.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 64

questions.q: Per the pediatric parameters table, what PEEP is suggested?
questions.exp: Pediatric PEEP 3–5 cmH2O.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 65

questions.q: Per the pediatric table, what peak inspiratory pressure limit applies in pressure control?
questions.exp: Pediatric PIP <28.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 65

questions.q: Per the pediatric table, inspiratory time ranges from:
questions.exp: Inspiratory time 0.4 (infants) to 1.0 (adolescents).
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 65

questions.q: Pediatric tidal volume per the lecture table is:
questions.exp: 5–8 mL/kg IBW with pressure support of 4–6 cmH2O.
questions.ref: Course materials: Anesthesia Ventilators: slide 65
